item.itunes:author: 小牛講正經
item.itunes:summary:

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入回顧2020年至2022年間，台灣疫情變化與關鍵防疫決策如何重塑國內政治版圖並左右首都選情。
  • 解析前衛福部長陳時中如何從聲勢頂峰的「防疫英雄」，轉變為背負施政包袱與民怨焦點的民進黨參選人。
  • 梳理2022年台北市長選戰前期的三腳督局勢，剖析蔣萬安、陳時中與黃珊珊初期的民調消長與選戰困境。

摘要

從防疫光環到民意轉折

作者回顧了2020年台灣面對COVID-19初期的情境。當時台灣創下連續253天零本土確診紀錄，每日下午兩點的疫情記者會成為全民焦點，時任衛福部長兼指揮中心指揮官的陳時中聲勢如日中天，全民掀起「順時中」風潮。在2020年4月的假想民調中，陳時中甚至以49%的支持度大幅領先國民黨立委蔣萬安，展現問鼎首都市長寶座的強大實力。

病毒變異引發的政策風暴與中央地方角力

然而，隨著病毒不斷變異，防疫神話面臨考驗。2021年Alpha變種病毒引爆諾富特飯店與機師群聚感染，在野黨強烈抨擊指揮中心放寬機組員檢疫為「3+11」的決策。隨後疫情蔓延至萬華引發全國三級警戒，官員稱萬華為「破口」更引發地方民怨。自此，中央與台北市展開激烈政治攻防，中央下午兩點召開記者會，台北市長柯文哲則於三點召開記者會分庭抗禮，雙方更圍繞在疫苗採購、國產高端疫苗與BNT疫苗爭議上針鋒相對。

共存轉型陣痛與2022首都選戰起跑

邁入2022年春季，傳染力強大的Omicron變種病毒肆虐，迫使指揮中心逐步放棄清零，轉向以減災為目標的「與病毒共存」。在政策急轉彎的過程中，伴隨快篩試劑短缺、停課與隔離標準反覆調整，以及餐飲觀光業重創，累積的民怨轉化為執政黨的沈重包袱。陳時中從昔日的抗疫領袖，逐漸成為政策代罪羔羊。此時年底地方大選戰鼓響起，對藍營而言，台北市已連續八年由非藍營執政，是絕不能再輸的關鍵戰役。

三強鼎立的初期選情與挑戰

國民黨於2022年5月正式徵召形象清新的立委蔣萬安參選。然而蔣萬安出線初期團隊步調緩慢、行程低調，被外界諷為「佛系選舉」與「躺平」，引發藍營基層焦慮。6月初公布的民調顯示，蔣萬安雖位居首位，但與因第一線防疫累積高聲量的副市長黃珊珊差距甚微，兩人落入誤差範圍；反觀陳時中則受本土疫情與防疫爭議衝擊滑落至第三名，首都市長爭奪戰正式進入緊繃的三腳督競逐。

================================================

Do you remember that summer five years ago when the COVID-19 pandemic broke out and all of Taiwan entered a Level 3 alert? "Oh, starting today, we are raising the national alert to Level 3." >> Although the Level 3 alert led to self-imposed lockdowns and empty streets everywhere, the daily number of confirmed cases did not drop significantly. >> Looking out at Nanwan Beach, there was nothing but sand; no people were there. In the blink of an eye, those days of. having to stay at home for self-isolation, wearing masks every time we went out, and scanning QR codes to report our whereabouts are already five years in the past. And this COVID-19 virus, which impacted the entire world, also impacted the election we are looking back at today. That's right, in our "Election History" video series, we have been reviewing Taipei mayoral elections since 1994. Today, we have reached the eighth episode: the 2022 Taipei mayoral election. First, let's take a time machine back to the spring of 2020. At that time, the pandemic was still in a controllable stage, and Taiwan even set a record of 253 consecutive days without any local cases. . Back then, Taiwan had a consistent peak in viewership; it wasn't the prime-time soap operas or variety shows , but the daily 2:00 PM pandemic press conference. The epidemic command center commander standing on the stage, speaking clearly and calmly, was the then-Minister of Health and Welfare, Chen Shih-chung. At that time, to cooperate with the efforts to keep local cases at zero, everyone talked about " following Chen Shih-chung," and the five officials at the command center were even dubbed the "Epidemic Prevention Dream Team." He wore a floral shirt to Kenting to promote the "New Lifestyle for Disease Prevention" campaign, and the floral shirt instantly saw a surge in inquiries, turning him into an unlikely viral marketing influencer. That April, TVBS conducted a. hypothetical poll for the Taipei mayoral race, and Chen Shih-chung took 49%, leaving KMT legislator Chiang Wan-an's 35%far behind. Suddenly, a pandemic commander became a top candidate for mayor of the capital city. All of this was built on the premise of completely blocking the entry of overseas cases. However, things soon took a sharp turn after the virus mutated. From the political bickering over whether Wanhua was the outbreak's origin, to the later chaos surrounding masks, rapid tests, and vaccines, as well as the policy contradiction between "Zero-COVID" and " living with the virus," the inconveniences people endured and the. economic impact finally erupted as collective public grievances at that moment. This battle against the pandemic went from a time when everyone was happy to "follow Chen Shih-chung" to becoming the ruling party's biggest political burden, ultimately becoming the key factor that influenced the 2022 local elections. By the way, the candidates ' academic theses have also become a major focus of public attention. Today, we will look back at the battle for the capital that followed the lifting of pandemic restrictions, discussing the fourth-generation pandemic commander and Ko Wen-je's successor. Who will be able to stand out in this race for the capital? Hello, I'm Xiao. Niu. Welcome to "Xiao Niu Talks Politics ." The story begins back in 2020 in Taiwan. During the early stages of the COVID-19 outbreak, Taiwan was consistently a global front-runner in epidemic prevention, but no matter how well we prepared, we couldn't keep up with the speed of viral mutations. By the end of 2020, the Alpha variant emerged, with a transmission rate 60% higher than the original COVID-19 virus . Just like that, the virus was quietly brought into the country, causing cluster infections. In late April, a cluster broke out at the Novotel hotel involving China Airlines pilots. Opposition parties pointed the finger at the Command Center for relaxing. quarantine rules for flight crews to "3 + 11"—three days of home quarantine followed by 11 days of self-health management. After the Novotel cluster spiraled out of control, the virus spread rapidly throughout the greater Taipei area, with Wanhua District—a densely populated area—starting to see confirmed cases of unknown origin. At the time, Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang’s remark calling Wanhua the "breakout point" infuriated the local residents. From that moment on, the greater Taipei area entered a Level 3 alert, and the central and local governments began an endless war of words. The Command Center held its usual 2 p.m. press conference, while the Taipei City Government held theirs.

at 3 p.m. Chen Shih-chung and Ko Wen-je became the main rivals in this pandemic arena, and the key point of contention was vaccines. Facing a vaccine shortage , opposition parties criticized the ruling DPP for using ideology to block imported vaccines in order to protect the domestic Medigen vaccine. For example, they slammed Chen Shih-chung for accusing the BNT vaccine of being repackaged in China during his testimony , calling it the spreading of misinformation. However, the DPP government insisted that with the whole world scrambling for vaccines and many middlemen involved, they had to stick to a government-to-government principle with original manufacturer authorization to ensure quality and avoid contract. disputes, especially regarding the BNT vaccine, which had to be shipped directly from the German factory. In the end, the pandemic had devolved into a situation where everyone was just talking past each other. Chen Shih-chung insisted that "3 + 11" was not the breakout point for the local outbreak, while Ko Wen-je threw down a harsh challenge, saying "we'll see what happens." Later, Ko scolded Chen for " not knowing what he's doing while drawing a paycheck," to which the DPP replied that emotional outbursts during the pandemic were entirely unnecessary. As the pandemic heated up, so did the rhetoric of politicians, naturally heightening anxiety among the public and making it increasingly difficult to separate pandemic prevention from. politics. By the spring of 2022, the Omicron variant struck, shifting the debate toward whether to "zero-out" or " coexist" with the virus. In early April , Chen Shih-chung admitted that a zero-COVID policy was no longer feasible . The central government set disaster reduction as the goal, effectively pivoting away from the zero-case target . However, during this policy U-turn, rapid test kits were in short supply, and quarantine and school suspension rules were constantly revised. Combined with the long-term border closures, the catering and tourism industries suffered immensely. At this point, Chen's role as commander became two-sided; to his supporters, he was the hero who led Taiwan through a once-in-a-century pandemic, but to. others, he was the face of the pandemic's toll. April 2022. The highly transmissible Omicron variant spread throughout the community. By April 30, daily confirmed cases exceeded 15,000. While transmission was rampant, the mortality rate was relatively low. The Command Center began rolling out relaxation policies, shortening home quarantine to "3 + 4" days and scrapping the SMS contact tracing system, all in hopes of accelerating a return to normal life. Meanwhile, as the pandemic began to ease , the drums of war for the year-end elections began to beat. For the "Blue" camp, Taipei had been without a Blue mayor for eight full years. In 2014, Sean Lien, and in 2018, Ting Shou-chung , both saw their vote shares stuck at around the 40%base. In 2018, the latter lost to Ko Wen-je by just over 3,000 votes. Therefore, the 2022 battle was one the KMT simply could not afford to lose. At the time, the candidate with the highest support within the party was , without question, Legislator Chiang Wan-an. With his bright, youthful appearance and credentials as a corporate lawyer, Chiang was much more marketable compared to the older generation of KMT heavyweights. He first won a legislative seat in Zhongshan and Beisongshan in 2016, and in 2020, he. successfully defended his seat and was re-elected despite the strong headwinds of the "Resist China, Protect Taiwan" movement. Of course, his family background is the most frequently mentioned topic; Chiang Wan-an's grandmother was Chang Ya-jo, and his father, Chiang Hsiao-yen, changed his surname to Chiang in 2005. He was originally named Chang Wan-an. He also changed his name accordingly, and the media often refers to him as the fourth generation of the Chiang family. This label helps him attract deep-blue voters , but it’s also destined to become a target for opponents. However, Chiang’s personality is truly too mild, even being mocked by pundits as "super soft and spineless." In May 2022, the KMT officially nominated him to run for Taipei mayor. His campaign slogan was " Your Taipei is Infinite," but for the next few weeks, Chiang had few public appearances, and his team was slow to assemble, leading everyone to call it a "Zen-style campaign" that had "laid flat ." Even the grassroots blue-camp members were anxious, forcing the party headquarters to dispatch experienced veteran staffers to come in and put out the fire. According to poll figures released by the media in early June, after Chiang formally announced his candidacy, there was no clear post-announcement bump. Although he took first place, the gap between him and second-place Huang Shan-shan was within the margin of error. Clearly, the high visibility from being at the forefront of pandemic prevention work allowed Huang Shan-shan to gain support from a.

segment of independent voters. As for Chen Shih-chung, he fell to third place . Outsiders also believe that the local outbreak and subsequent controversies related to pandemic prevention clearly placed a heavy negative burden on him. Coupled with the DPP's inability to confirm who would run, the stance of green-camp supporters became conservative. For the DPP, how should they resolve the situation with their once-presumed ace starting pitcher, who is now a struggling hitter? Since Chen Shui-bian failed his re-election bid in 1998, the DPP has not governed the capital for 24 years. However, during this period, President Tsai Ing-wen twice achieved the feat of winning over half the votes in Taipei City, meaning Taipei citizens aren't necessarily anti-DPP by default; it’s just that the prerequisite is that the candidate must possess the charisma to attract independent voters. At the time, those named as potential candidates for Taipei. mayor included the so-called "two Chens and one Lin": pandemic commander Chen Shih-chung, former Vice President Chen Chien-jen, and former Minister of Transportation Lin Chia-lung, who was the first to announce his bid. The problem was that the DPP's top choice, Chen Shih-chung, simply couldn't get away. In the spring of 2022, as the Omicron pandemic heated up, Chen Shih-chung always prioritized epidemic prevention when asked about running for office. Party leaders also wanted him to lead the command center until the pandemic subsided, arguing that managing the epidemic was essential for election prospects. However, others believed that resigning early was the only way to exit the battlefield sooner; the longer he stayed, the heavier the burden of the. pandemic would become, and no one could say for sure when it would end. Because of this, the nomination schedule was dragged on by the pandemic until July, and the party headquarters' final decision process was a total reshuffling of the deck. On July 10th, the DPP’s election committee recommended drafting Chen Shih-chung to run for Taipei mayor , while Lin Chia-lung, who had been actively preparing for Taipei, shifted his focus to New Taipei City. Chen Shih-chung subsequently submitted his resignation at the Executive Yuan meeting, ending his 1,985-day tenure as the longest-serving Minister of Health and Welfare in nearly 25 years. Regarding his run for Taipei mayor, Chen declared, "When responsibility comes, I will carry it." His fan page received 40,000 likes just four hours after launching. Supporters of the pan-green. camp had been restless for a long time, finally waiting for their "Minister Ah-Chung" to step up against the then-popular Chiang Wan-an and Taipei Deputy Mayor Huang Shan-shan, who had been a constant media focus during the pandemic. Shortly after Chen announced his candidacy, the China Times published poll numbers that made everyone gasp: Chen at 24.2%, Chiang at 23.9%, and Huang at 22.2%. All three were squeezed within the margin of error; this wasn't just a tight race—it was practically a three-way pile-up! Chen Shih-chung’s entry immediately boosted the momentum of the pan-green camp, while Huang Shan-shan’s numbers proved her grassroots strength and appeal to centrist voters, making her not so. easily sidelined. Of course, facing Chen’s transition into a mayoral candidate, his opponents were never going to just sit on the sidelines. Chiang Wan-an immediately blasted Chen as the first commander in the history of the Republic of China’s epidemic prevention efforts to "run away." Ko Wen-je also accused Chen of disregarding national safety. However, the first card Chen played was to apologize to Wanhua residents for the "Wanhua as a breakout point" remark made by then-Deputy Minister Shih Chung-liang, hoping to proactively resolve this painful point that his opponents kept attacking. But that wasn't the only painful point. Just in July, an academic ethics scandal originating from Hsinchu became a major. blow to the pan-green camp. The main figure in this political storm is Lin Chih-chien, who just left his position as Mayor of Hsinchu to run for Mayor of Taoyuan. On July 5th, KMT Taipei City Councilor Wang Hung-wei held a press conference accusing Lin Chih-chien's Chung Hua University master's thesis of plagiarism. The next day, KMT councilors also reported Lin to NTU, alleging his National Development Institute thesis was highly similar to one written half a year earlier by Yu Cheng-huang, an investigator at the Investigation Bureau. This time bomb, involving academic ethics, was officially ignited. Lin Chih-chien insisted there was no plagiarism, claiming his survey outline and writing.

were done earlier than Yu's, and that he had shared the data in good faith. Their shared advisor, current National Security Bureau Director Chen Ming-tung , also claimed he modified Lin's thesis first and gave it to Yu for reference, denying any plagiarism. Regarding Lin's claims, Yu Cheng-huang refuted them through his lawyer, stating he wrote his thesis according to academic standards. He personally attended NTU’s review committee to explain, while NTU invited Lin and Chen three times during the process. Both of them failed to attend. In response, Lin Chih-chien emphasized that the review committee chair, Su Hung-dah, was biased due to his close. ties to the KMT and had already labeled the controversy a scandal, so he requested a new chair. However, NTU ignored Lin’s request. On August 9th, NTU announced the results: the similarity between the two theses exceeded 40%. Since Yu’s thesis was completed six months earlier and Lin had even cited it, NTU concluded Lin had committed serious plagiarism and revoked his master's degree. This heavy blow effectively ended Lin's political career , and on August 12th, he announced his withdrawal from the Taoyuan mayoral race , vowing to defend his innocence on another battlefield. Unexpectedly, less than a month later, Chung Hua University. released its own review, concluding that Lin’s master's thesis there did indeed plagiarize a report from the Science Park Administration, and likewise revoked his master's degree. From that moment on, plagiarism instantly became a standard for scrutinizing political figures. Everyone began frantically digging through their opponents 'theses , running them through software to check for plagiarism. It wasn't just the Green camp caught in the storm; caught up in the fallout along with Lin was KMT Hsinchu mayoral candidate Lin Keng-jen, who also had his master's degree revoked after his school determined his thesis was plagiarized. Has the fire of this plagiarism scandal reached Taipei? Opinions are divided. Some believe that Taipei citizens care about academic backgrounds, so Chen Shih-chung would surely be swept up in the storm; however , looking at the data, his polling numbers remained largely unaffected. The true impact of the thesis case was on the DPP’s overall election prospects across Taiwan, defined by the question: "Do you trust NTU, or do you trust the DPP?" Beyond the plagiarism controversy , it was a case of "when it rains, it pours." On July 22, 2022, the Hsinchu Municipal Baseball Stadium, renovated for 1.2 billion during Lin Chih-chien's term, opened to great fanfare. Yet,. after just two games, three players were injured, and Lin Che-hsuan's season was cut short. Safety concerns sparked questions, leading the CPBL and the Wei Chuan Dragons to move remaining games back to Tianmu Stadium. The stadium became another battleground for the Blue , Green, and White camps, with Kao Hung-an's mayoral campaign mocking that "hidden treasures" were buried in the field. The spread of the plagiarism scandal and the "abysmal project" label on the stadium dealt a direct blow to the Green camp’s momentum. At this moment, the White camp, representing Ko Wen-je, played its cards, deciding to have Deputy Mayor Huang Shan-shan run. for Taipei mayor as an independent. Huang became a lawyer at 23, was elected a Taipei city councilor at 28 for the New Party, later joined the PFP, and served six terms. In 2019, she was recruited by Ko Wen-je as deputy mayor, becoming known as his successor. However , her position was awkward: she is James Soong's protégé and a PFP member, yet backed by Ko’s TPP. This led her to run as an independent, hoping to avoid embarrassing the PFP while replicating Ko’s 2014 success to maximize the centrist vote. On August 28, Huang announced her. candidacy in her stronghold, Neihu. Dressed in white, she joked about her name, saying she was "arriving late"( Shan-shan) but had been preparing for 24 years. She proclaimed a "citizen-first" doctrine, arguing the best way to topple the blue-green wall is to elect Huang Shan-shan. The day after her announcement, a TVBS poll showed Chiang Wan-an and Huang Shan-shan both at 26%, with Chen Shih-chung at 23%, narrowing the gap between Chiang and Huang from the original 10%to just 3%. Even more surprising is that among voters aged 30 to 39, nearly half support Huang Shan-shan. For the Blue camp, they are facing enemies on both sides; attacking.

Chen Shih-chung benefits Huang, but attacking Huang risks offending Ko's supporters, cutting off their retreat path. It’s a similar headache for the Green camp, as Chen, backed by the party , still lagged in the August polls. Three candidates. As each candidate announced their run for Taipei mayor, policy became a key point of contention , and the first battlefield was the traffic in Neihu. Previously, due to Ko Wen-je’s remark that "Neihu traffic is beyond saving," the gridlock during rush hour has become a major battlefield in every mayoral election. Chen Shih-chung proposed solutions as soon as he announced his run. These four solutions. for Neihu's traffic include building new highway ramps and digging a tunnel under the Keelung River using shallow excavation methods; however, Huang Shan-shan poured cold water on these ideas. She argued that the biggest bottleneck in Neihu is actually Songshan Airport. In the long run, moving the airport would allow for new connecting bridges. She also criticized the DPP for only discussing moving the airport during mayoral elections. Chen responded that throwing out such big issues during a campaign is more about political posturing than municipal development. Interestingly, four years later, incumbent Chiang Wan-an, seeking re-election, also proposed a vision to abolish the airport and build an AI park . In any case, this prime piece of land at Songshan Airport seems to spark. everyone's imagination in almost every election. Speaking of Chiang Wan-an, his bus policy also left him red-faced. After his suggestion of booking bus seats online was mocked as impractical, he proposed doing 20 squats in exchange for a free bus ride. Although he claimed he was just citing someone else's idea, this whimsical notion was immediately mocked by Ko Wen-je, who remarked that it was about the level he expected from him. Meanwhile, the Chen campaign, aiming to woo young and female voters, visited bars, danced hip-hop, and held pink parties. While some saw him as letting his guard down, others felt it. was too forced. It created a huge disconnect from the steady, commander-in-chief image Chen had previously cultivated. Of course, when creativity is poorly handled, it can backfire badly; the most classic example being Chen Shih-chung’s bidet toilet advertisement. Shortly after announcing his candidacy, Chen Shih-chung proposed a "public restroom upgrade" policy, aiming to install bidet seats in the 7,200 restrooms managed by the Taipei City Government, hoping to mirror Japan and effectively improve the service quality of Taipei’s public facilities. Although both the KMT and TPP camps criticized the policy for its low feasibility, the initial intent was good . However, the advertisement launched by his team to promote this policy featured. Chen imitating a viral meme, showing him peeking over a restroom partition and flashing a peace sign at an internet celebrity inside. 摘要

從防疫光環到民意轉折

作者回顧了2020年台灣面對COVID-19初期的情境。當時台灣創下連續253天零本土確診紀錄，每日下午兩點的疫情記者會成為全民焦點，時任衛福部長兼指揮中心指揮官的陳時中聲勢如日中天，全民掀起「順時中」風潮。在2020年4月的假想民調中，陳時中甚至以49%的支持度大幅領先國民黨立委蔣萬安，展現問鼎首都市長寶座的強大實力。

病毒變異引發的政策風暴與中央地方角力

邁入2022年春季，傳染力強大的Omicron變種病毒肆虐，迫使指揮中心逐步放棄清零，轉向以減災為目標的「與病毒共存」。在政策急轉彎的過程中，伴隨快篩試劑短缺、停課與隔離標準反覆調整，以及餐飲觀光業重創，累積的民怨轉化為執政黨的沈重包袱。陳時中從昔日的抗疫領袖，逐漸成為政策代罪羔羊。此時年底地方大選戰鼓響起，對藍營而言，台北市已連續八年由非藍營執政，是絕不能再輸的關鍵戰役。

In the spring of 2022, as the Omicron pandemic heated up, Chen Shih-chung always prioritized epidemic prevention when asked about running for office. Party leaders also wanted him to lead the command center until the pandemic subsided, arguing that managing the epidemic was essential for election prospects. However, others believed that resigning early was the only way to exit the battlefield sooner; the longer he stayed, the heavier the burden of the. pandemic would become, and no one could say for sure when it would end. Because of this, the nomination schedule was dragged on by the pandemic until July, and the party headquarters' final decision process was a total reshuffling of the deck. On July 10th, the DPP’s election committee recommended drafting Chen Shih-chung to run for Taipei mayor , while Lin Chia-lung, who had been actively preparing for Taipei, shifted his focus to New Taipei City. Chen Shih-chung subsequently submitted his resignation at the Executive Yuan meeting, ending his 1,985-day tenure as the longest-serving Minister of Health and Welfare in nearly 25 years. Regarding his run for Taipei mayor, Chen declared, "When responsibility comes, I will carry it." His fan page received 40,000 likes just four hours after launching. Supporters of the pan-green. camp had been restless for a long time, finally waiting for their "Minister Ah-Chung" to step up against the then-popular Chiang Wan-an and Taipei Deputy Mayor Huang Shan-shan, who had been a constant media focus during the pandemic. Shortly after Chen announced his candidacy, the China Times published poll numbers that made everyone gasp: Chen at 24.2%, Chiang at 23.9%, and Huang at 22.2%. All three were squeezed within the margin of error; this wasn't just a tight race—it was practically a three-way pile-up! Chen Shih-chung’s entry immediately boosted the momentum of the pan-green camp, while Huang Shan-shan’s numbers proved her grassroots strength and appeal to centrist voters, making her not so. easily sidelined. Of course, facing Chen’s transition into a mayoral candidate, his opponents were never going to just sit on the sidelines. Chiang Wan-an immediately blasted Chen as the first commander in the history of the Republic of China’s epidemic prevention efforts to "run away." Ko Wen-je also accused Chen of disregarding national safety. However, the first card Chen played was to apologize to Wanhua residents for the "Wanhua as a breakout point" remark made by then-Deputy Minister Shih Chung-liang, hoping to proactively resolve this painful point that his opponents kept attacking. But that wasn't the only painful point. Just in July, an academic ethics scandal originating from Hsinchu became a major. blow to the pan-green camp. The main figure in this political storm is Lin Chih-chien, who just left his position as Mayor of Hsinchu to run for Mayor of Taoyuan. On July 5th, KMT Taipei City Councilor Wang Hung-wei held a press conference accusing Lin Chih-chien's Chung Hua University master's thesis of plagiarism. The next day, KMT councilors also reported Lin to NTU, alleging his National Development Institute thesis was highly similar to one written half a year earlier by Yu Cheng-huang, an investigator at the Investigation Bureau. This time bomb, involving academic ethics, was officially ignited. Lin Chih-chien insisted there was no plagiarism, claiming his survey outline and writing.

were done earlier than Yu's, and that he had shared the data in good faith. Their shared advisor, current National Security Bureau Director Chen Ming-tung , also claimed he modified Lin's thesis first and gave it to Yu for reference, denying any plagiarism. Regarding Lin's claims, Yu Cheng-huang refuted them through his lawyer, stating he wrote his thesis according to academic standards. He personally attended NTU’s review committee to explain, while NTU invited Lin and Chen three times during the process. Both of them failed to attend. In response, Lin Chih-chien emphasized that the review committee chair, Su Hung-dah, was biased due to his close. ties to the KMT and had already labeled the controversy a scandal, so he requested a new chair. However, NTU ignored Lin’s request. On August 9th, NTU announced the results: the similarity between the two theses exceeded 40%. Since Yu’s thesis was completed six months earlier and Lin had even cited it, NTU concluded Lin had committed serious plagiarism and revoked his master's degree. This heavy blow effectively ended Lin's political career , and on August 12th, he announced his withdrawal from the Taoyuan mayoral race , vowing to defend his innocence on another battlefield. Unexpectedly, less than a month later, Chung Hua University. released its own review, concluding that Lin’s master's thesis there did indeed plagiarize a report from the Science Park Administration, and likewise revoked his master's degree. From that moment on, plagiarism instantly became a standard for scrutinizing political figures. Everyone began frantically digging through their opponents 'theses , running them through software to check for plagiarism. It wasn't just the Green camp caught in the storm; caught up in the fallout along with Lin was KMT Hsinchu mayoral candidate Lin Keng-jen, who also had his master's degree revoked after his school determined his thesis was plagiarized. Has the fire of this plagiarism scandal reached Taipei? Opinions are divided. Some believe that Taipei citizens care about academic backgrounds, so Chen Shih-chung would surely be swept up in the storm; however , looking at the data, his polling numbers remained largely unaffected. The true impact of the thesis case was on the DPP’s overall election prospects across Taiwan, defined by the question: "Do you trust NTU, or do you trust the DPP?" Beyond the plagiarism controversy , it was a case of "when it rains, it pours." On July 22, 2022, the Hsinchu Municipal Baseball Stadium, renovated for 1.2 billion during Lin Chih-chien's term, opened to great fanfare. Yet,. after just two games, three players were injured, and Lin Che-hsuan's season was cut short. Safety concerns sparked questions, leading the CPBL and the Wei Chuan Dragons to move remaining games back to Tianmu Stadium. The stadium became another battleground for the Blue , Green, and White camps, with Kao Hung-an's mayoral campaign mocking that "hidden treasures" were buried in the field. The spread of the plagiarism scandal and the "abysmal project" label on the stadium dealt a direct blow to the Green camp’s momentum. At this moment, the White camp, representing Ko Wen-je, played its cards, deciding to have Deputy Mayor Huang Shan-shan run. for Taipei mayor as an independent. Huang became a lawyer at 23, was elected a Taipei city councilor at 28 for the New Party, later joined the PFP, and served six terms. In 2019, she was recruited by Ko Wen-je as deputy mayor, becoming known as his successor. However , her position was awkward: she is James Soong's protégé and a PFP member, yet backed by Ko’s TPP. This led her to run as an independent, hoping to avoid embarrassing the PFP while replicating Ko’s 2014 success to maximize the centrist vote. On August 28, Huang announced her. candidacy in her stronghold, Neihu. Dressed in white, she joked about her name, saying she was "arriving late"( Shan-shan) but had been preparing for 24 years. She proclaimed a "citizen-first" doctrine, arguing the best way to topple the blue-green wall is to elect Huang Shan-shan. The day after her announcement, a TVBS poll showed Chiang Wan-an and Huang Shan-shan both at 26%, with Chen Shih-chung at 23%, narrowing the gap between Chiang and Huang from the original 10%to just 3%. Even more surprising is that among voters aged 30 to 39, nearly half support Huang Shan-shan. For the Blue camp, they are facing enemies on both sides; attacking.

Chen Shih-chung benefits Huang, but attacking Huang risks offending Ko's supporters, cutting off their retreat path. It’s a similar headache for the Green camp, as Chen, backed by the party , still lagged in the August polls. Three candidates. As each candidate announced their run for Taipei mayor, policy became a key point of contention , and the first battlefield was the traffic in Neihu. Previously, due to Ko Wen-je’s remark that "Neihu traffic is beyond saving," the gridlock during rush hour has become a major battlefield in every mayoral election. Chen Shih-chung proposed solutions as soon as he announced his run. These four solutions. for Neihu's traffic include building new highway ramps and digging a tunnel under the Keelung River using shallow excavation methods; however, Huang Shan-shan poured cold water on these ideas. She argued that the biggest bottleneck in Neihu is actually Songshan Airport. In the long run, moving the airport would allow for new connecting bridges. She also criticized the DPP for only discussing moving the airport during mayoral elections. Chen responded that throwing out such big issues during a campaign is more about political posturing than municipal development. Interestingly, four years later, incumbent Chiang Wan-an, seeking re-election, also proposed a vision to abolish the airport and build an AI park . In any case, this prime piece of land at Songshan Airport seems to spark. everyone's imagination in almost every election. Speaking of Chiang Wan-an, his bus policy also left him red-faced. After his suggestion of booking bus seats online was mocked as impractical, he proposed doing 20 squats in exchange for a free bus ride. Although he claimed he was just citing someone else's idea, this whimsical notion was immediately mocked by Ko Wen-je, who remarked that it was about the level he expected from him. Meanwhile, the Chen campaign, aiming to woo young and female voters, visited bars, danced hip-hop, and held pink parties. While some saw him as letting his guard down, others felt it. was too forced. It created a huge disconnect from the steady, commander-in-chief image Chen had previously cultivated. Of course, when creativity is poorly handled, it can backfire badly; the most classic example being Chen Shih-chung’s bidet toilet advertisement. Shortly after announcing his candidacy, Chen Shih-chung proposed a "public restroom upgrade" policy, aiming to install bidet seats in the 7,200 restrooms managed by the Taipei City Government, hoping to mirror Japan and effectively improve the service quality of Taipei’s public facilities. Although both the KMT and TPP camps criticized the policy for its low feasibility, the initial intent was good . However, the advertisement launched by his team to promote this policy featured. Chen imitating a viral meme, showing him peeking over a restroom partition and flashing a peace sign at an internet celebrity inside. It was likely intended to be funny, but it reminded many netizens of a scene from a Korean film, turning a comedic attempt into something creepy. Although Chen Shih-chung quickly issued a public apology and took the video down, commentators bluntly pointed out that this was a very clear policy blunder. Following that, it was time to dig up old grievances, as the main battlefield for the three candidates returned to the issue of vaccines. In mid-August, the KMT legislative caucus revealed that documents related to vaccine procurement. were sealed for 30 years. Chiang Wan-an immediately launched an attack, questioning how one could trust Chen to manage a city budget of over 100 billion NTD annually when things were so opaque . The Chen camp retorted that 30 years is the standard retention period for major procurement documents, meaning they must be kept for 30 years, not that they cannot be disclosed for 30 years. They accused Chiang Wan-an of knowing the truth, given that he himself is the convener of the Legislative Yuan's vaccine investigation committee. However , the most damaging blow came from an unexpected bombshell thrown from the sidelines. In mid-September, veteran media personality Chou Yu-kou used her talk show to expose the lesser-known past of the Chiang family, ranging from the mystery of Chiang Wan-an’s ancestry to his father Chiang Hsiao-yen’s. extramarital affair from over 20 years ago. Faced with these media attacks, the usually mild-mannered Chiang took a firm stance: "If you have the guts, come after me directly; don't drag other people into this." But what really caused the situation to spiral out of control was on September 22nd, when Chou Yu-kou and another media figure, Tsai Yu-chen, directly named former Miss China Chang Shu-chuan as the woman involved in the affair during their program. The next day, Chang went to the Taipei District Prosecutors Office to file a lawsuit, tearfully recounting how she had been bullied and slandered. Unexpectedly, Chou appeared on the scene claiming she wanted to apologize to Chang in person, only to end up in a shouting match with City Councilor Wang Hung-wei, who was accompanying Chang, with both sides calling each other cockroaches and rats. This scene was.

later seen as a turning point that affected the election, and in this instance, it was actually Chen Shih-chung who ended up taking the hit. It is widely believed that Chou Yu-kou and Chen Shih-chung have a good relationship, leading many politicians to immediately declare that "supporting Chen Shih-chung is supporting Chou Yu-kou." Huang Shan-shan also stepped forward to support Chiang Wan-an, asking them if they had any conscience at all. Heart and conscience. As for Chen Shih-chung, he came forward to soften the situation, suggesting that everyone is an independent individual responsible for their own words. Although everyone made their corresponding stances known, in this wave of smear tactics, the real beneficiary was Chiang Wan-an, which was immediately reflected in the poll numbers. According to a TVBS poll in. early October, Chiang Wan-an's support jumped to 40%, Huang Shan-shan's was 23 %, and Chen Shih-chung's was 22%. Regarding this case, the Taipei District Prosecutors Office also indicted Chou and Tsai. In the latest second-instance verdict, Chou Yu-kou was sentenced to nine months, and Tsai Yu-chen... Entering the final month of the election , all three sides began to play their trump cards. On October 1st, Chen Shih-chung established his campaign headquarters, with Pan-Green heavyweights like Tsai Ing-wen, Lai Ching-te, Su Tseng-chang, and Chen Chien-jen all in attendance. On the same day, the KMT mobilized Chu Li-lun, Ma Ying-jeou, and Hou Yu-ih to secure the base for Chiang. As for Huang Shan-shan's side, former New Power Party chairman Huang Kuo-chang, who had not. yet joined the Taiwan People's Party, declared: "If I were a Taipei citizen, I would definitely vote for Huang Shan-shan." As the Blue and Green camps returned to their ranks and the base began to mobilize, the response rate in polls significantly increased. Chen Shih-chung's poll numbers saw an uptick , shaking off his entanglement with Huang Shan-shan. According to the early November poll by Formosa Magazine, Chiang Wan-an stood at 34.3%, Chen Shih-chung at 27.7%, and Huang Shan-shan at 22.4%, widening the gap between the three and making Chiang Wan-an's advantage more obvious. Now everyone is asking the same question: will there be "strategic voting"? Sure enough, the master of strategic voting, Broadcasting Corporation of China chairman Jaw. Shaw-kong, immediately made a move: the KMT supporting the TPP's Kao Hung-an in Hsinchu in exchange for the TPP supporting Chiang Wan-an in Taipei. Huang Shan-shan bitterly criticized Jaw Shaw-kong for engaging in naked political bartering, but this rhetoric did not have much impact on her polling situation. As mentioned earlier, Huang Shan-shan's voter base does not necessarily come from the Blue camp; a large portion consists of light-green supporters, and combined with her personal appeal, centrist voters are willing to buy in. These highly autonomous supporters are not easily swayed like those of Wang Chien-shien or James Soong in the past, who were eventually victims of strategic voting. On October 5th, the only televised debate of the entire election campaign. took place. Before the debate, everyone expected Huang Shan-shan, who is relatively familiar with municipal affairs, to perform better, believing she might dominate the stage and overshadow Chiang Wan-an and Chen Shih-chung. Unexpectedly, on the day of the debate, Chiang Wan-an put on his glasses and displayed a confident and fluent demeanor, which was in stark contrast to his past "soft" reputation. This sharp contrast left everyone with the impression that he performed much better than expected. As for Chen Shih-chung, he focused on an emotional appeal. Faced with overwhelming criticism regarding pandemic prevention and vaccine procurement, he directly appealed to emotions in his closing statement. He said, "I wanted to protect. everyone in Taiwan, but I failed to do so. I'm sorry, and thank you all for your hard work." Scholars analyzed this as an attempt to seek understanding and empathy from the citizens. He wanted to convey that even if he didn't succeed, he had worked hard. However, the day after the debate, KMT councilor Hsu Chiao-hsin released photos she claimed were provided by the public, accusing Chen of allegedly hugging and holding hands with a married female deputy hospital superintendent, portraying him as a "groping hand." Chen's campaign headquarters refuted Hsu's narrative, stating that there was no sign of any groping or sexual harassment in the photos. Regardless, the damage to Chen. Shih-chung from these leaked photos was already done. Official polls showed Chiang Wan-an at 36%, Chen Shih-chung at 25%, and Huang Shan-shan at 24%, showing that the gap between Chiang and Chen had widened once again. Even more subtle was the age demographic in the polls. In the TVBS final poll, 56%of those aged 20 to 29 supported Huang Shan-shan. CommonWealth Magazine also found that in polls over the last two months, Chen Shih-chung never led in this age group. The support of young people remained firmly with Ko Wen-je and Huang Shan-shan, which became a major reason why "strategic voting" was difficult to achieve. Finally, on the eve of the election, it rained heavily in Taipei. Chiang called out in the rain for.

everyone to embrace Taipei and Taiwan. Chen Shih-chung teared up on stage, saying those were tears shed because the achievements of pandemic prevention were smeared during the campaign. Huang Shan-shan chose the plaza in front of City Hall, also in the pouring rain, urging citizens to defend new values and break away from old forces. In this three-way race that fought bitterly from the end of the pandemic, who would finally emerge victorious? On the voting day of November 26th, the voter turnout in Taipei was about 68%, which is not considered high compared to previous elections. Once the votes were tallied, Chiang’s lead grew steadily throughout the night. Around 7:00 PM, Chen Shih-chung was the first to concede, inviting his supporters to join him in. wishing Chiang Wan-an well and expressing hope that the smear campaigns against pandemic prevention efforts would end there. When Huang Shan-shan addressed the crowd for her concession speech, she gave Mayor Ko Wen-je an emotional hug, thanking him for his mentorship and encouragement. At 8:00 PM , Chiang walked onto the stage to cheers of "Mr. Mayor," stating that citizens had used their votes to let kindness triumph over malice. He thanked his opponents, Chen and Huang, for their efforts. His father, Chiang Hsiao-yen, who had remained unseen throughout the campaign, appeared on stage at the final moment to give his son a big hug. In the final count, Chiang secured 570,000 votes, a 42%share; Chen Shih-chung took 430,000 votes, about 32%; and Huang. Shan-shan received 340,000 votes, totaling 25%. At 43 years old, Chiang was elected mayor of Taipei, becoming the youngest directly elected mayor in the city’s history. However, Chiang’s vote share was the lowest for a KMT candidate elected in Taipei, and Chen failed to secure the traditional Pan-Green base, performing only slightly better than Yao Wen-chih in 2018. The key factor was Huang Shan-shan; although she received far fewer votes than Ko Wen-je did four years ago, she was not completely squeezed out, holding onto a quarter of the total vote. Why did Chen Shih-chung lose? I believe his greatest asset and his biggest burden were actually the same thing: his role in pandemic prevention. Supporters remember. the commander who stood on stage at 2:00 PM sharp for over 900 days, but for other voters, memories of Wanhua, the " 3 + 11" policy, and vaccine issues were resurfaced throughout the campaign. Fairly speaking, many decisions made during the pandemic by all camps were made under time pressure with incomplete information; merits and faults are hard to summarize, but an election is a single-choice question, not a performance review. Add to that the controversies surrounding the social media team and the fallout from the Hsu Chun-chi incident, and it became difficult for Chen to expand his support in the final stage. As for Huang Shan-shan, although she captured most of the independent voters and had the lowest "negativity rating" of the three. , the approval rating for the Ko administration remained low, failing to garner enough praise for municipal performance to expand her base. Her final vote count was 240,000 lower than when Ko was re-elected four years ago. And why did Chiang Wan-an win? His personality was criticized for being too soft or timid, but he held firm to the Pan-Blue base. While their opponents were mired in controversy, they steadily caught every ball, eventually hitting a seemingly routine but title-winning strike by relying on the Blue-Silver Turtle tower. The repercussions of this election extended far beyond Taipei; the DPP failed to win any of the five northern Keelung and Taoyuan cities, and. Tsai Ing-wen announced her resignation as party chair that very night. As for Huang Shan-shan, she officially joined the TPP the following year, and her quarter of the vote signaled that Taipei was no longer under the sole control of the Blue and Green parties. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入回顧2020年至2022年間，台灣疫情變化與關鍵防疫決策如何重塑國內政治版圖並左右首都選情。
  • 解析前衛福部長陳時中如何從聲勢頂峰的「防疫英雄」，轉變為背負施政包袱與民怨焦點的民進黨參選人。
  • 梳理2022年台北市長選戰前期的三腳督局勢，剖析蔣萬安、陳時中與黃珊珊初期的民調消長與選戰困境。

摘要

從防疫光環到民意轉折

作者回顧了2020年台灣面對COVID-19初期的情境。當時台灣創下連續253天零本土確診紀錄，每日下午兩點的疫情記者會成為全民焦點，時任衛福部長兼指揮中心指揮官的陳時中聲勢如日中天，全民掀起「順時中」風潮。在2020年4月的假想民調中，陳時中甚至以49%的支持度大幅領先國民黨立委蔣萬安，展現問鼎首都市長寶座的強大實力。

病毒變異引發的政策風暴與中央地方角力

然而，隨著病毒不斷變異，防疫神話面臨考驗。2021年Alpha變種病毒引爆諾富特飯店與機師群聚感染，在野黨強烈抨擊指揮中心放寬機組員檢疫為「3+11」的決策。隨後疫情蔓延至萬華引發全國三級警戒，官員稱萬華為「破口」更引發地方民怨。自此，中央與台北市展開激烈政治攻防，中央下午兩點召開記者會，台北市長柯文哲則於三點召開記者會分庭抗禮，雙方更圍繞在疫苗採購、國產高端疫苗與BNT疫苗爭議上針鋒相對。

共存轉型陣痛與2022首都選戰起跑

邁入2022年春季，傳染力強大的Omicron變種病毒肆虐，迫使指揮中心逐步放棄清零，轉向以減災為目標的「與病毒共存」。在政策急轉彎的過程中，伴隨快篩試劑短缺、停課與隔離標準反覆調整，以及餐飲觀光業重創，累積的民怨轉化為執政黨的沈重包袱。陳時中從昔日的抗疫領袖，逐漸成為政策代罪羔羊。此時年底地方大選戰鼓響起，對藍營而言，台北市已連續八年由非藍營執政，是絕不能再輸的關鍵戰役。

三強鼎立的初期選情與挑戰

國民黨於2022年5月正式徵召形象清新的立委蔣萬安參選。然而蔣萬安出線初期團隊步調緩慢、行程低調，被外界諷為「佛系選舉」與「躺平」，引發藍營基層焦慮。6月初公布的民調顯示，蔣萬安雖位居首位，但與因第一線防疫累積高聲量的副市長黃珊珊差距甚微，兩人落入誤差範圍；反觀陳時中則受本土疫情與防疫爭議衝擊滑落至第三名，首都市長爭奪戰正式進入緊繃的三腳督競逐。

================================================

Do you remember that summer five years ago when the COVID-19 pandemic broke out and all of Taiwan entered a Level 3 alert? "Oh, starting today, we are raising the national alert to Level 3." >> Although the Level 3 alert led to self-imposed lockdowns and empty streets everywhere, the daily number of confirmed cases did not drop significantly. >> Looking out at Nanwan Beach, there was nothing but sand; no people were there. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 從味全龍奪冠重返榮耀的畫面出發，回顧龍象對決的經典與遺憾。
  • 梳理味全企業的家族背景與球隊興衰，理解商業決策如何改變一支球隊的命運。
  • 重現黃平洋在總冠軍賽中的驚人表現，感受台灣職棒初期的拚戰精神與代價。

摘要

龍象首度在冠軍賽交鋒，味全龍重返榮耀

作者以2026年台灣大賽第六戰開場：味全龍在第八局由捕手蔣宏擊出全壘打，最終以四勝二敗擊敗中信兄弟，奪下總冠軍。這是中職史上首次由「龍象」兩支元老球隊在總冠軍賽交手，也讓球迷再次想起味全龍的興衰與重生。

作者回顧，味全龍曾在1990年代與兄弟象形成經典對抗，卻在強盛之際遭到解散。1999年，味全企業以職棒簽賭風波為由停掉球隊，魏家接手後更正式解散球隊；但球迷也知道，食品事業虧損與職棒票房前景不佳，才是球隊走入歷史的重要背景。當年數千名龍迷冒著寒風上街抗議，成為台灣職棒史上首次球迷為球隊發起的遊行。二十年後，魏家又讓味全龍重返球場，使球迷不禁思索：今日的紅色，是否仍等同於記憶中的味全龍？

味全企業的家族根源與棒球緣起

故事回到企業創辦人黃烈火。1939年，他在日本神戶創立合泰商會，戰後將事業帶回台灣並取得豐田代理權，發展為和泰汽車；1953年，他成立生產味精的公司，隔年改名為味全。味全食品從味精拓展至醬油、罐頭、奶粉與果汁，成為台灣第一家上市食品公司，曾與統一分據市場南北。

黃家與蘇家共同經營和泰、味全等事業，家族版圖涵蓋汽車、食品、房地產與金融。然而，黃烈火兩房所生的長子黃克銘與黃南圖年齡相差十餘歲、關係疏遠，而兩人的家族脈絡也與味全龍的命運緊密相連。1978年，台中宜寧高中棒球隊因經費不足面臨解散，味全原本只打算資助一學期，球隊卻接連奪下全國冠軍與世界青棒賽冠軍，促使味全進一步投入青棒，並與文化大學合作培育成棒隊伍。

紅軍登場與職棒初代霸業

1988年中華職棒籌組期間，味全積極布局，不只計畫在埔頂牧場興建球場，也招攬海外球員與業餘名將黃平洋。1990年職棒正式開打，身穿紅衣的「紅軍」味全龍登上職棒舞台。當年四月的龍象戰吸引一萬六千名觀眾，創下聯盟首次滿場紀錄，從此成為票房保證。

味全龍首季由黃平洋、洋投史提夫・翁提維洛斯與性格火爆的荷西・紐內茲組成投手「三本柱」，三人合計拿下球隊52勝中的46勝。龍隊在總冠軍賽迎戰兄弟象，黃平洋於第六戰完投完封，助球隊以四勝二敗奪得中職史上第一座總冠軍，也點燃台灣職棒熱潮。

黃平洋的連戰紀錄與極限考驗

作者特別介紹被稱為「金臂人」的黃平洋。他擅長多種變化球，因球路繁多而有「七彩變化球」之稱；加入味全首年便身兼先發與後援，投出246局、拿下20勝，工作量遠超現代職棒常態。

1991年總冠軍賽，味全龍與統一獅展開勢均力敵的「食品大戰」。黃平洋第一戰投131球完投勝，休息三天後又在第四戰投滿14局、用球182顆，雖遭再見安打仍繼續扛起重任。第六戰他再度登板，以130球完封、僅被敲三支安打，將系列賽逼進第七戰；不到24小時後，先發投手提早退場，他又上場救援。耗盡體力的黃平洋最終遭統一獅擊出11支安打，這段賽事既凸顯他的傳奇，也呈現當年投手承受的沉重負荷。

On the evening of October 26, 2026, at the Taipei Dome, during the bottom of the eighth inning of Game 6 of the Taiwan Series, Wei Chuan Dragon catcher Chiang Hung hits a home run. Nine. With the final out recorded in the top of the ninth, red streamers rained down from the stands as the Wei Chuan Dragons defeated the CTBC Brothers four games to two to win the 2026 CPBL championship. This was the first time in. the 37-year history of the CPBL that a " Dragon vs. Elephant" showdown took place in the championship series. These two original teams battled for a full decade in the 90s, with fans shouting at each other in the stands, yet they never once met in the finals. Why? Because just as the Dragons were at their strongest, the team was shut down by their own owner. Rewinding 27 years to December 1999, shortly after the Wei Chuan Dragons completed a three-peat, the parent company suspended the team, and soon after, shut it down entirely, officially disbanding them. The reason was the sensational gambling scandal in professional baseball at the time; the new owners, the Wei brothers, felt. heartbroken, asking, "Why should I run a casino for people to gamble in?" That sentence became the final straw for the Wei Chuan Dragons. Although everyone knew the losses from the Wei Chuan food business and the bleak outlook for CPBL ticket sales were the real reasons this championship dynasty was consigned to history. At the time, thousands of Dragon fans braved the cold wind to take to the streets; this was the first time in Taiwan's professional baseball history that fans marched for their team . Why did this team reach such a point? Some blame the new owners, the Wei family, while others say the old owner, the Ho family, was the real culprit. Ironically, the same Wei family that. shut down the team 20 years ago is the one that brought them back to life 20 years later. Fans have mixed feelings; there is a certain shade of red in one's life—can the red of today really be equated to the red of the Wei Chuan Dragons from 20 years ago? In this episode, we will talk about the story of the Wei Chuan Dragons, an original CPBL team that disappeared and has now returned to the scene. Before we begin the story, I would like to ask everyone to please click that subscribe button. Subscribing is easy for you and won't affect your YouTube homepage algorithm at all, but for us, the subscriber count is the most tangible encouragement and helps us get noticed by potential. sponsors! If one person subscribes, one person is happy; if 300,000 people subscribe, 300,000 people are happy! Let's grow together, welcome to "Little Cow Talks Business." To start the story , let's first talk about a man named Huang Lieh-ho. In 1939, Huang Lieh-ho opened a trading company called Ho-Tai Shokai in Kobe, Japan. After World War II, he moved his business back to Taiwan and secured the agency rights for Toyota , which is the Ho-Tai Motor we all know today. In 1953, he founded a company producing MSG called "Ho-Tai Chemical Industry," and renamed it "Wei-Chuan" the following year, which is the well-known Wei-Chuan Foods today. Wei-Chuan expanded from MSG into soy sauce, canned goods, powdered milk, and fruit juice, becoming Taiwan's first publicly listed food company. Before Uni-President appeared, Taiwan's food market was almost entirely dominated by Wei-Chuan. It wasn't until Uni-President grew later that the saying "Wei-Chuan in the North, Uni-President in the South" emerged. Back then, the Ho-Tai and Wei-Chuan groups were jointly run by the Huang family and their relatives, the Su family. The Huangs managed food, while the Sus managed cars. With the second generation of the Huangs adding construction, leasing, and securities, their business empire covered automotive , food, real estate, and finance. Calling the Huang family a prestigious. business dynasty in Taiwan is no exaggeration at all. However, this prestigious family had turbulent undercurrents. Huang Lie-huo had two wives; the eldest son of the first wife was Huang Ke-ming, and the eldest son of the second wife was Huang Nan-tu. The two brothers were more than a decade apart in age and grew up separately, so their relationship remained quite distant. You should remember these two names, as the fate of the Wei-Chuan Dragons is closely tied to these brothers. Wei-Chuan’s connection to baseball began in 1978. At that time, the baseball team at Taichung’s Yin-Ning High School was facing disbandment due to funding difficulties, so the school sought help from Wei-Chuan through a referral. Wei-Chuan, at the time,. decided to sponsor the team for one semester with a charitable mindset. Unexpectedly, this investment helped Yin-Ning High School not only win the national title but also take home the championship trophy at the World Youth Baseball Tournament, making Wei-Chuan an overnight sensation. Because of this, they decided to invest deeply in youth baseball. In July of the same year, they signed a collaborative agreement with Chinese Culture University, allowing high school graduates to pursue their studies while continuing to play ball. This group of people became the founding members of the Wei-Chuan adult baseball team. In 1988, Brother Hotel chairman Hung Teng-sheng began traveling everywhere to establish a professional baseball league. Besides Brother Hotel,.

other companies that expressed interest included Uni-President, Evergreen, and Wei-Chuan. Wei-Chuan acted very quickly ; they not only planned to build a stadium on their own Wei-Chuan Puding Ranch but also began reaching out to overseas players like Yang Chieh-jen and Lin Yi-tseng. Weiquan later signed the biggest star from the amateur leagues, pitcher Huang Ping-yang. At the time, the Japan Express team offered him an annual salary equivalent to over 2 million NTD to keep him, but Huang ultimately chose to return to Taiwan, even though the highest monthly salary in the entire CPBL that year was only 80,000 NTD. Just like that, with the official start of the Chinese Professional Baseball League in 1990, the "Red Army," dressed in all red, made. their official debut on the professional stage. On March 17, 1990, the very first game of the CPBL was played at the now-demolished Taipei Municipal Baseball Stadium. The Dragon-Elephant showdown on April 29th set a record as the first sell-out in league history. 16,000 fans packed the stadium, and even the light poles outside were crowded with people trying to catch a glimpse; from then on , the Dragon-Elephant rivalry became a box-office guarantee. That year, the Weiquan Dragons were powered by the first "Big Three" in Taiwanese professional baseball history: the " Golden Arm" Huang Ping-yang, the outstanding foreign pitcher "General" Steve Ontiveros, and the slick-haired, hot-tempered "Bad Boy" Jose Nunez, who would throw things on the sidelines whenever he was upset. That year, the Dragons achieved 52 wins, with these three pitchers accounting for 46 of them . Ontiveros was the league's first foreign pitcher to reach double-digit wins and the first to win a Monthly MVP , eventually taking the ERA title with a 1.92. Nunez, on the other hand, was the complete opposite of the reserved Ontiveros; he chewed gum, wore gold earrings, and most importantly, rarely listened to his catcher's signs, throwing whatever he wanted. If he wasn't satisfied with his performance after leaving the mound, he would kick the clubhouse door—he was a foreign pitcher with a very distinct style. As. the second-half champions of the inaugural season, the Dragons faced the Brother Elephants in the Taiwan Series. Huang Ping-yang pitched a nine-inning shutout in Game 6, and the Dragons ultimately won 4-2 to claim the first championship trophy in CPBL history, igniting the professional baseball craze in Taiwan. At this point, we must talk more about this "Golden Arm" Huang Ping-yang. Expert in various breaking pitches, he had so many types that he was nicknamed the "Seven-Colored Breaking Ball." After joining the Weiquan Dragons in that first year, he became the team's ace, working both as a starter and a reliever, ultimately pitching a total of 246 innings and racking up 20 wins. By today's baseball standards, this frequency of play is an. astronomical figure, yet Huang was still able to dominate the game. What truly turned Huang Ping-yang into a legend was the following year, the 1991 championship series. That year featured a "food war" between the Taipei-based Weichuan Dragons and the Southern powerhouse Uni-President Lions. Both teams had an identical record of 46 wins that season, showing how evenly matched their strength was. In Game 1, the Dragons naturally sent out their local ace, Huang Ping-yang, who threw 131 pitches to secure a complete-game victory. Then, in Game 4, Huang took the mound again after just three days of rest. In that game, he pitched a full 14 innings—yes, you heard that right, 14 innings—using 182 pitches. Worst of all. , he ended up giving up a walk-off hit to the Lions. That pitch count was truly terrifying. But the most terrifying part was yet to come. In Game 6, with only a short rest, he threw another 130 pitches for a complete-game shutout, allowing only three hits, successfully pushing the series to a do-or-die Game 7. Fans who witnessed it all in person said that Huang was already completely exhausted, with his fastball velocity dropping to just over 130 km/h, yet he still managed to mix in various breaking balls to keep the Lions 'hitters guessing. But the series wasn't over, and Huang still couldn't rest. In Game 7, when the. starting pitcher was pulled early, the person who came on in relief was—you saw that right—Huang Ping-yang again. With less than 24 hours of rest, he was back on the clock, but this time, he could no longer hold them off. With his energy bar completely drained, Huang stood on the mound like the goalkeeper from the movie "Shaolin Soccer," getting battered by the Lions for 11 hits and giving up seven runs. Even so, he gritted his teeth and pitched over three innings before finally checking out of the game . In one single series, Huang appeared in four games and threw a total of 522 pitches. Even then, he couldn't stop the Lions, and he could only watch in sorrow. as they triumphed in the "food war." The result of such inhumane management was that Huang's arm immediately broke down . In 1995, he flew to the U.S. for Tommy John ligament replacement surgery. Even more cruelly, despite being injured and recovering for the team, the organization actually asked him to take a pay cut twice during that period. When he finally made his comeback in 1996, his salary hadn't increased by a single cent, remaining at the same 210,000 NTD monthly wage as before his injury. Perhaps it was this feeling of being taken for granted that led Huang Ping-yang to leave the Wei-Chuan Dragons in late 1996, defecting to the Taiwan.

Major League along with several teammates. At this point, his speed was gone and his performance wasn't what it used to be, but he was still in Taiwan. He secured his 100th career win with the TML's Sun team, becoming the third player in professional baseball history to reach the century mark. However, when the two leagues merged three years later , he refused to pay the redemption fee to return to the CPBL, choosing instead to leave professional baseball to open a railway bento shop in Tianmu, and was later elected as a Taipei City Councilor . An ace who once shouldered the entire Wei-Chuan Dragons team, he moved on without hesitation. In January 1991, the Dragons handed the head coaching position to 32-year-old Hsu Sheng-ming,. who became the youngest head coach at the time. Hsu’s managing style was highly unconventional, and his animated behavior on the sidelines quickly made him a fixture in the news; in his first year, he encountered the "6/1 Incident" that brought him instant fame. On June 1st, during a game between the Dragons and the Brothers at Taipei Municipal Baseball Stadium, rain began to fall in the middle innings. Hsu felt the delay had exceeded the allowed time and the game should be called, but officials ignored him, so he ordered his team to pack up and leave the field. The fans were furious; soda cans and bentos weren't enough, so they ripped out stadium seats and threw them onto the. field. This was the first fan riot in CPBL history. Just how divided were the Dragons and Brothers fans? Hsu’s wife, Hsieh Jung-yao, later recalled that she knew exactly which market stalls belonged to Dragons fans and which to Brothers fans, and would intentionally avoid them to avoid getting cold shoulders while shopping. Whenever the Dragons lost, Coach Hsu would be lectured on his tactics by street vendors while accompanying his wife to the market the next day. It seems the " armchair manager" existed even back then . In July of that same year, Dragons submarine pitcher Yang Chieh-jen threw the first no-hitter in CPBL history against the San-Hoo, using his deceptive pitches to stymie them and earning the. nickname "Tiger-Slaying Hero." He joined the Yomiuri Giants in 1988, hitting a home run in his first at-bat in the majors, immediately becoming known as the " Asian Great Cannon" and a household name in Taiwan, though his later career didn't go as expected and he struggled with the Giants. In 1991, he decided to return to Taiwan to play professional baseball, specifically wanting to return to his old team from the Wei-Chuan era. The problem was that the Chinese Professional Baseball League had a draft system. If Lu Ming-Tzu wanted to join a CPBL team, he had to follow the rules and enter the draft, and it was the Brothers who held the first overall pick. that year. In order to secure this " Asian slugger," the Wei-Chuan Dragons decided to make the first move, signing Lu to a hitting coach contract with a monthly salary of 200,000, hoping to get a head start. The other three teams were , of course, unhappy about this. The Brothers even threatened to cancel all upcoming "Dragons vs. Brothers" games, refusing to play against Wei-Chuan on the same field. After much negotiation, Lu Ming-Tzu ultimately had to enter the draft, and as expected, he was selected by the Brothers who held the top pick, even though he still preferred to join the Dragons. This stalemate was finally broken when the Dragons' stolen base king, Lin Yi-Tseng, volunteered to be traded to the Brothers, allowing Lu Ming-Tzu to fulfill his wish and wear. the Dragons 'jersey. And so, before the 1992 spring training, the Dragons traded Lin Yi-Tseng and catcher Chen Yen-Cheng to acquire Lu Ming-Tzu, marking the first player trade in the history of the league. Everyone knows what happened next: Lin Yi-Tseng went to the Brothers , experienced their three-peat, and after retiring, became a manager and led them to another three-peat. As for Lu Ming-Tzu, he did not quite live up to the "slugger" hype everyone expected. Entering the mid-90s, the off-field drama of the Wei-Chuan Dragons was even more theatrical than the games on the field! On the field, the Brother Elephants won three consecutive titles from 1992 to 1994, and the league expanded to six teams in 1993. The " Dragons vs. Brothers" rivalry remained the biggest draw in the league, but the Dragons' performance didn't show much improvement, and they could never beat the Brothers 'submarine pitcher, Chen Hsien-Chang. For 505 days, they couldn't get a single win against him, and Chen earned the nickname "Dragonslayer." As for the off-field situation, we must return to the Wei-Chuan brothers we mentioned earlier and asked you to remember. In 1986, Wei-Chuan founder Huang Lieh-ho handed the business over to his half-brothers: the elder Huang Ke-ming as Chairman and the second son Huang Nan-tu as General Manager. It looked like a standard family succession , but because their personalities were polar opposites—one conservative and one. aggressive—they struggled to reconcile their decision-making, leading to nine years of unhappy coexistence. By 1995, Huang Nan-tu teamed up with market investors to force his older brother out and take over as chairman, but this was akin to inviting outsiders into the family, leading to increasingly diluted family shareholding. Starting in 1996, Wei Chuan fell into consecutive years of losses. As the company hit hard times, the players were the first to feel the impact. In early 1996, the Wei Chuan Dragons adjusted salaries, with an average team increase of only 8%. Some veterans even faced pay cuts, earning less than incoming rookies. Key players like Tseng Chih-mao, Lo Shih-hsin, and.

Yang Chieh-jen went to the Wei Chuan building on Songjiang Road to confront the management. Chairman Chen Chin-kuang simply replied with a Taiwanese idiom, implying that once the company made money, everyone would naturally get a share—though not everyone would get to share in it. At that time, pitcher Lin Guang-hung directly asked for his release from the Dragons. He admitted that another professional league currently in formation had already approached him, and the "other league" he referred to was the Taiwan Major League, founded by Chiu Fu-sheng of the Era Group. In September 1996, they announced an investment of 200 million NT dollars to sign a group of stars from CPBL teams like Wei Chuan and. Uni-President. In December of the same year, five Wei Chuan stars—Huang Ping-yang, Kuo Chien-lin, Sun Chao-li, Li An-hsi, and Kaiser—officially announced they were jumping ship to the Taiwan Major League. Lu Ming-tzu also left Wei Chuan during this wave. According to reports from netizens, Liang Kung-pin, a key figure in the Taiwan Major League at the time, revealed on his podcast that even before the match-fixing scandal, the Wei Chuan management had already lost interest in the team, and with poor compensation, it was no wonder their stars were so easily poached. Of course, some fans argued that Huang Nan-tu had at least publicly promised to continue operations, and the players who stayed the following year. actually received significant raises, but the real storm was yet to come. In early 1997, prosecutors questioned several China Times Eagles players, triggering the Black Eagles match-fixing scandal. At the same time, the Taiwan Major League officially began. A small Taiwan was suddenly packed with 11 professional teams, two leagues, and two sets of schedules. Coupled with frequent rumors of game-throwing, fans would constantly have a question in their minds when entering the stadium: Is this game actually real? It was at this moment that the stands began to empty, marking the official entry into a dark era. And yet, the Wei Chuan Dragons dynasty happened to be right in the middle of this professional baseball. winter. In 1996, the Wei Chuan Dragons’ roster began a generational transition. The team signed 19-year-old trainee Chang Tai-shan through a special tryout . He won the Rookie of the Year award right away and was dubbed the "Prince of the Forest." Yeh Chun-chang, who would later become their star catcher, also joined that same year. The Dragons won the second-half season title, but after reaching the Taiwan Series, they once again returned home empty-handed. In 1997, the Dragons surged in the second half of the season, relying on several powerful foreign players to clinch the second-half title. In the Taiwan Series , they faced the Chinatrust Whales, a team that had just survived the Black Eagles scandal where most of their players were implicated and replaced by loaners from other teams. From the third. game on, the Dragons staged a comeback, winning four consecutive games and securing the championship in Tainan. During those years, the Dragons had the former league batting champion Chen Chin-mao, foreign player Dardo who stole 71 bases in a single season, and the dominant closer Garcia, who pitched 45 consecutive scoreless innings. He was betting that no one in Taiwan would be willing to pay that much for Wei Chuan, and that if the market investors were saddled with heavy interest payments, they would eventually collapse. Little did he expect that someone would strike from across the strait. The Wei family of Yongjing, Changhua—who made their fortune in China with Master Kong instant noodles—the Ting Hsin International Group, led by the four brothers Wei Ying-chou, Wei Ying-chiao, Wei Ying-chung, and Wei Ying-heng, stepped in and bought out the market investors' entire stake at a price even higher than what Ah Ding had demanded. Ting Hsin eventually secured more than half of the board seats, gaining actual control over Wei Chuan. Originally, Ting Hsin intended to keep Huang Nan-tu as. chairman, but the Huang family vetoed it themselves, even removing him from the family's list of directors. Just like that, Wei Chuan, which Huang Lieh-huo had founded and managed for 45 years, officially transitioned from a family business of the Huangs to the Wei family . It is said that when the news was announced, 89-year-old Huang Lieh-huo was devastated for a long time, even wanting to buy Wei Chuan back at any cost, but unfortunately, there were no " what-ifs"—a momentary mistake led to eternal regret. That year, Wei Chuan only ranked third in the regular season , relying on the playoffs to defeat Uni-President and squeeze into the championship series. In the finals, their opponent was the Sinon Bulls, anchored by a powerful lineup of sluggers. However, thanks to pitching.

coach Yang Chieh-jen’s strategies, they neutralized Sinon's power hitters and successfully won the championship, completing a back-to-back title run. But off the field, Wei Chuan wasn't as lucky ; in the second half of 1998, Wei Chuan's stock price plummeted. According to reports from that time, the holdings of the Su and Huang families had dropped to less than 2%, as they prepared to pull out of Wei Chuan entirely. Regardless, entering 1999, Wei Chuan had effectively become a company belonging to the Ting Hsin Group. 1999 began with turmoil. On April 18, Hsu Sheng-ming became the league’s first manager to reach 300 wins, but eight days later, he was stabbed by thugs in. front of his home, becoming the first manager in the league to be injured due to mafia intimidation. On September 20, a game between the Sinon Bulls and the Wei Chuan Dragons drew only 101 spectators. There were more birds in the stands than people, setting a record for the lowest attendance in professional baseball history. Just hours after this game filled with birds ended, the 921 earthquake struck. This natural disaster dealt another heavy blow to an already struggling professional baseball environment. Amid this cold winter for pro baseball, Wei Chuan made it to the championship series again against the Mercuries Tigers, but the series turned out to be unusually heated. In Game 1,. Wei Chuan slugger Ta-ti-shih collided with Mercuries catcher Wang Kuang-hui at home plate. The two got into an argument and a fight broke out. After things finally calmed down, a second brawl erupted in the ninth inning. This incident made the Dragons-Tigers series the most violent championship series in history. This brawl brought the championship series to a climax, as the Wei Chuan Dragons ultimately defeated the Mercuries Tigers four games to one, successfully completing their three-peat dynasty. But very quickly, the high tide was immediately followed by a low ebb. Just one day before the Dragons won the title, the Tigers had already announced their disbandment, and the future of the Dragons, whose parent company was also. suffering heavy losses, remained uncertain. That very night, Hsu Sheng-ming pleaded with the team organization, "You absolutely cannot disband the team!" They then proceeded as planned on their championship trip to Europe, but they were unaware that internally, Wei Chuan had already reached its verdict. According to reports at the time, the Dragons were losing 80 to 90 million a year, and Wei Chuan Corporation had lost over a billion in just the first three quarters of 1999, with stock prices plummeting below 10 dollars, turning into " dumpling stock." Disbanding the team had long been the internal consensus; reports even suggested that if they hadn't won the championship this year, the announcement would have come during the season. On October 30th, just three. weeks after their three-peat, the Wei Chuan Dragons announced a one-year hiatus. The organization emphasized this wasn't a disbandment, claiming coaches and players would still receive 60%of their salaries and the team would return to the CPBL once the environment improved. However, the CPBL naturally did not accept such a vague suspension and demanded that Wei Chuan clearly state whether they were playing or not. When the word "disbandment" finally came up, the fans were heartbroken and began organizing online. On December 12th, a group calling itself the "Save the Dragons" association launched a protest march, calling not just for the team to stay, but for a clean professional league and improvements to the draft. system and stadium facilities. This was the first time in Taiwan's professional baseball history that fans took to the streets for a team, but what was on the mind of Wei Chuan's new boss, Wei Ying-hsing? According to reports, after winning the title, he heard someone say : "The Dragons only won the championship because others threw the games for them ." It was this very sentence that deeply wounded Wei Ying-hsing’s heart. He asked , "Why should I spend money to run a casino for people to gamble?" Organized crime, drugs, and game-fixing—these dark clouds hanging overhead became a major reason for Wei Ying-hsing to disband the team. Sure enough, the next morning on December 13th, the Wei family called team leader Ren Zhongjie to a meeting. and made the final decision to disband. Ren held a press conference that afternoon to announce the sad news. Manager Hsu Sheng-ming, who led the team to a three-peat, was in disbelief and said this to the camera. " >> Hmm, when we won the championship, those were tears of victory. These are truly tears of regret. Honestly, so I just said something that might not sound very comfortable to the Wei family, but I still have to say it.""We left the Huang family only to come to the Wei family, and that’s when we realized the Huang family was actually much better. It sounds harsh, but I still have to say it ." >> At the dissolution press conference that afternoon, the scene was nearly chaotic ! Fans wrote on a whiteboard: "Wei Chuan. is deceiving fans 'feelings; boycott Wei Chuan products." Some people tore up posters and stomped on them, while others sobbed by the door. Some fans asked directly, "If there are financial problems, just be honest. Why blame the professional baseball environment?" Someone even asked the most stinging question: "Why? Was the three-peat real or fake?"" >> So, you cannot ask me whether it was real or fake." "You have to ask the teams that played against us or look at the games throughout the season to see if they were real or not." At that time, some players still hoped that the Farglory Group, or even their old owners, the Huang family and the Su family of Hotai.

, would step in to take over. But in the end, no one showed up. The Dragons had to go their separate ways; Yeh Chun-chang and Chang Tai-shan later transferred to the Sinon Bulls. The CPBL shrunk from six teams back to its original four. Ultimately, who exactly killed the Wei Chuan Dragons? Public criticism of the Wei family was direct: they spent a fortune to buy the Wei Chuan company, only to make the team vanish into thin air at its absolute peak with a single decision. Many loyal fans decided from that day on that they would never buy Wei Chuan products again . However, another group of fans believes that the Huang family was actually the original culprit. Their reasoning is that during the later period of Huang's management, the team had long been neglected. Huang Ping-yang. was even asked to take a pay cut after his surgery. When the A-League (Naruwan ) stepped in, they poached a large number of key players. Losing management rights and selling off shares only made their financial situation worse. When the team disbanded, players waited desperately for their old owners to return, but the Huangs and the Sus never made a move. Some even believe that Hsu Sheng-ming's famous quote was originally meant to complain about the Huang family , only to find that the Wei family was even more disappointing. From my perspective, both arguments hold some truth, but neither tells the whole story . With the league split, the 921 earthquake, and the financial crisis, Taiwanese professional baseball back then was essentially in ruins. Internal. conflicts laid the groundwork, the Wei family made the final decision, and the broader environment pushed the team toward collapse. How did the fans—who had lost their team—spend those 20 years ? After the team disbanded, the official site and forums stopped updating, so the fans taught themselves to build a site from scratch, creating a place called the "Dragon League" to give dispersed fans a home. And the ones behind this revival were none other than the Ting Hsin Wei family, the very ones who had dealt the final blow to the team years ago. It wasn't until early 2019 that the plan was finally restarted; as soon as the news broke, people online began saying, "Ting Hsin is buying an indulgence this time." The regrets of those years and the remorse of that time seem to have been. put to rest. In 2021, the Dragons returned to the major league , making Tianmu Baseball Stadium their home field. To bolster their roster, they signed former MLB pitcher Wang Wei-chung to a five-year contract worth over 60 million, making him the bona. fide "Dragon King." At the draft the following year, they also added the slugger Giljegiljaw Kungkuan. At this moment, 20 years of bitterness and waiting transformed into the joy of victory. Manager Yeh Chun-chang also wept, saying, "Because it’s the Dragons , many past memories flooded my mind, so.

it feels very different." It is precisely because the Dragons won the championship that those 20 years of regrets experienced by the fans could finally be truly put to rest. 摘要

龍象首度在冠軍賽交鋒，味全龍重返榮耀

作者以2026年台灣大賽第六戰開場：味全龍在第八局由捕手蔣宏擊出全壘打，最終以四勝二敗擊敗中信兄弟，奪下總冠軍。這是中職史上首次由「龍象」兩支元老球隊在總冠軍賽交手，也讓球迷再次想起味全龍的興衰與重生。

作者回顧，味全龍曾在1990年代與兄弟象形成經典對抗，卻在強盛之際遭到解散。1999年，味全企業以職棒簽賭風波為由停掉球隊，魏家接手後更正式解散球隊；但球迷也知道，食品事業虧損與職棒票房前景不佳，才是球隊走入歷史的重要背景。當年數千名龍迷冒著寒風上街抗議，成為台灣職棒史上首次球迷為球隊發起的遊行。二十年後，魏家又讓味全龍重返球場，使球迷不禁思索：今日的紅色，是否仍等同於記憶中的味全龍？

味全企業的家族根源與棒球緣起

故事回到企業創辦人黃烈火。1939年，他在日本神戶創立合泰商會，戰後將事業帶回台灣並取得豐田代理權，發展為和泰汽車；1953年，他成立生產味精的公司，隔年改名為味全。味全食品從味精拓展至醬油、罐頭、奶粉與果汁，成為台灣第一家上市食品公司，曾與統一分據市場南北。

黃家與蘇家共同經營和泰、味全等事業，家族版圖涵蓋汽車、食品、房地產與金融。然而，黃烈火兩房所生的長子黃克銘與黃南圖年齡相差十餘歲、關係疏遠，而兩人的家族脈絡也與味全龍的命運緊密相連。1978年，台中宜寧高中棒球隊因經費不足面臨解散，味全原本只打算資助一學期，球隊卻接連奪下全國冠軍與世界青棒賽冠軍，促使味全進一步投入青棒，並與文化大學合作培育成棒隊伍。

紅軍登場與職棒初代霸業

1988年中華職棒籌組期間，味全積極布局，不只計畫在埔頂牧場興建球場，也招攬海外球員與業餘名將黃平洋。1990年職棒正式開打，身穿紅衣的「紅軍」味全龍登上職棒舞台。當年四月的龍象戰吸引一萬六千名觀眾，創下聯盟首次滿場紀錄，從此成為票房保證。

味全龍首季由黃平洋、洋投史提夫・翁提維洛斯與性格火爆的荷西・紐內茲組成投手「三本柱」，三人合計拿下球隊52勝中的46勝。龍隊在總冠軍賽迎戰兄弟象，黃平洋於第六戰完投完封，助球隊以四勝二敗奪得中職史上第一座總冠軍，也點燃台灣職棒熱潮。

黃平洋的連戰紀錄與極限考驗

作者特別介紹被稱為「金臂人」的黃平洋。他擅長多種變化球，因球路繁多而有「七彩變化球」之稱；加入味全首年便身兼先發與後援，投出246局、拿下20勝，工作量遠超現代職棒常態。

1991年總冠軍賽，味全龍與統一獅展開勢均力敵的「食品大戰」。黃平洋第一戰投131球完投勝，休息三天後又在第四戰投滿14局、用球182顆，雖遭再見安打仍繼續扛起重任。第六戰他再度登板，以130球完封、僅被敲三支安打，將系列賽逼進第七戰；不到24小時後，先發投手提早退場，他又上場救援。耗盡體力的黃平洋最終遭統一獅擊出11支安打，這段賽事既凸顯他的傳奇，也呈現當年投手承受的沉重負荷。
