Wei-Chuan expanded from MSG into soy sauce, canned goods, powdered milk, and fruit juice, becoming Taiwan's first publicly listed food company. Before Uni-President appeared, Taiwan's food market was almost entirely dominated by Wei-Chuan. It wasn't until Uni-President grew later that the saying "Wei-Chuan in the North, Uni-President in the South" emerged. Back then, the Ho-Tai and Wei-Chuan groups were jointly run by the Huang family and their relatives, the Su family. The Huangs managed food, while the Sus managed cars. With the second generation of the Huangs adding construction, leasing, and securities, their business empire covered automotive , food, real estate, and finance. Calling the Huang family a prestigious. business dynasty in Taiwan is no exaggeration at all. However, this prestigious family had turbulent undercurrents. Huang Lie-huo had two wives; the eldest son of the first wife was Huang Ke-ming, and the eldest son of the second wife was Huang Nan-tu. The two brothers were more than a decade apart in age and grew up separately, so their relationship remained quite distant. You should remember these two names, as the fate of the Wei-Chuan Dragons is closely tied to these brothers. Wei-Chuan’s connection to baseball began in 1978. At that time, the baseball team at Taichung’s Yin-Ning High School was facing disbandment due to funding difficulties, so the school sought help from Wei-Chuan through a referral. Wei-Chuan, at the time,. decided to sponsor the team for one semester with a charitable mindset. Unexpectedly, this investment helped Yin-Ning High School not only win the national title but also take home the championship trophy at the World Youth Baseball Tournament, making Wei-Chuan an overnight sensation. Because of this, they decided to invest deeply in youth baseball. In July of the same year, they signed a collaborative agreement with Chinese Culture University, allowing high school graduates to pursue their studies while continuing to play ball. This group of people became the founding members of the Wei-Chuan adult baseball team. In 1988, Brother Hotel chairman Hung Teng-sheng began traveling everywhere to establish a professional baseball league. Besides Brother Hotel,.

other companies that expressed interest included Uni-President, Evergreen, and Wei-Chuan. Wei-Chuan acted very quickly ; they not only planned to build a stadium on their own Wei-Chuan Puding Ranch but also began reaching out to overseas players like Yang Chieh-jen and Lin Yi-tseng. Weiquan later signed the biggest star from the amateur leagues, pitcher Huang Ping-yang. At the time, the Japan Express team offered him an annual salary equivalent to over 2 million NTD to keep him, but Huang ultimately chose to return to Taiwan, even though the highest monthly salary in the entire CPBL that year was only 80,000 NTD. Just like that, with the official start of the Chinese Professional Baseball League in 1990, the "Red Army," dressed in all red, made. their official debut on the professional stage. On March 17, 1990, the very first game of the CPBL was played at the now-demolished Taipei Municipal Baseball Stadium. The Dragon-Elephant showdown on April 29th set a record as the first sell-out in league history. 16,000 fans packed the stadium, and even the light poles outside were crowded with people trying to catch a glimpse; from then on , the Dragon-Elephant rivalry became a box-office guarantee. That year, the Weiquan Dragons were powered by the first "Big Three" in Taiwanese professional baseball history: the " Golden Arm" Huang Ping-yang, the outstanding foreign pitcher "General" Steve Ontiveros, and the slick-haired, hot-tempered "Bad Boy" Jose Nunez, who would throw things on the sidelines whenever he was upset. That year, the Dragons achieved 52 wins, with these three pitchers accounting for 46 of them . Ontiveros was the league's first foreign pitcher to reach double-digit wins and the first to win a Monthly MVP , eventually taking the ERA title with a 1.92. Nunez, on the other hand, was the complete opposite of the reserved Ontiveros; he chewed gum, wore gold earrings, and most importantly, rarely listened to his catcher's signs, throwing whatever he wanted. If he wasn't satisfied with his performance after leaving the mound, he would kick the clubhouse door—he was a foreign pitcher with a very distinct style. As. the second-half champions of the inaugural season, the Dragons faced the Brother Elephants in the Taiwan Series. Huang Ping-yang pitched a nine-inning shutout in Game 6, and the Dragons ultimately won 4-2 to claim the first championship trophy in CPBL history, igniting the professional baseball craze in Taiwan. At this point, we must talk more about this "Golden Arm" Huang Ping-yang. Expert in various breaking pitches, he had so many types that he was nicknamed the "Seven-Colored Breaking Ball." After joining the Weiquan Dragons in that first year, he became the team's ace, working both as a starter and a reliever, ultimately pitching a total of 246 innings and racking up 20 wins. By today's baseball standards, this frequency of play is an. astronomical figure, yet Huang was still able to dominate the game. What truly turned Huang Ping-yang into a legend was the following year, the 1991 championship series. That year featured a "food war" between the Taipei-based Weichuan Dragons and the Southern powerhouse Uni-President Lions. Both teams had an identical record of 46 wins that season, showing how evenly matched their strength was. In Game 1, the Dragons naturally sent out their local ace, Huang Ping-yang, who threw 131 pitches to secure a complete-game victory. Then, in Game 4, Huang took the mound again after just three days of rest. In that game, he pitched a full 14 innings—yes, you heard that right, 14 innings—using 182 pitches. Worst of all. , he ended up giving up a walk-off hit to the Lions. That pitch count was truly terrifying. But the most terrifying part was yet to come. In Game 6, with only a short rest, he threw another 130 pitches for a complete-game shutout, allowing only three hits, successfully pushing the series to a do-or-die Game 7. Fans who witnessed it all in person said that Huang was already completely exhausted, with his fastball velocity dropping to just over 130 km/h, yet he still managed to mix in various breaking balls to keep the Lions 'hitters guessing. But the series wasn't over, and Huang still couldn't rest. In Game 7, when the. starting pitcher was pulled early, the person who came on in relief was—you saw that right—Huang Ping-yang again. With less than 24 hours of rest, he was back on the clock, but this time, he could no longer hold them off. With his energy bar completely drained, Huang stood on the mound like the goalkeeper from the movie "Shaolin Soccer," getting battered by the Lions for 11 hits and giving up seven runs. Even so, he gritted his teeth and pitched over three innings before finally checking out of the game . In one single series, Huang appeared in four games and threw a total of 522 pitches. Even then, he couldn't stop the Lions, and he could only watch in sorrow. as they triumphed in the "food war." The result of such inhumane management was that Huang's arm immediately broke down . In 1995, he flew to the U.S. for Tommy John ligament replacement surgery. Even more cruelly, despite being injured and recovering for the team, the organization actually asked him to take a pay cut twice during that period. When he finally made his comeback in 1996, his salary hadn't increased by a single cent, remaining at the same 210,000 NTD monthly wage as before his injury. Perhaps it was this feeling of being taken for granted that led Huang Ping-yang to leave the Wei-Chuan Dragons in late 1996, defecting to the Taiwan.

Major League along with several teammates. At this point, his speed was gone and his performance wasn't what it used to be, but he was still in Taiwan. He secured his 100th career win with the TML's Sun team, becoming the third player in professional baseball history to reach the century mark. However, when the two leagues merged three years later , he refused to pay the redemption fee to return to the CPBL, choosing instead to leave professional baseball to open a railway bento shop in Tianmu, and was later elected as a Taipei City Councilor . An ace who once shouldered the entire Wei-Chuan Dragons team, he moved on without hesitation. In January 1991, the Dragons handed the head coaching position to 32-year-old Hsu Sheng-ming,. who became the youngest head coach at the time. Hsu’s managing style was highly unconventional, and his animated behavior on the sidelines quickly made him a fixture in the news; in his first year, he encountered the "6/1 Incident" that brought him instant fame. On June 1st, during a game between the Dragons and the Brothers at Taipei Municipal Baseball Stadium, rain began to fall in the middle innings. Hsu felt the delay had exceeded the allowed time and the game should be called, but officials ignored him, so he ordered his team to pack up and leave the field. The fans were furious; soda cans and bentos weren't enough, so they ripped out stadium seats and threw them onto the. field. This was the first fan riot in CPBL history. Just how divided were the Dragons and Brothers fans? Hsu’s wife, Hsieh Jung-yao, later recalled that she knew exactly which market stalls belonged to Dragons fans and which to Brothers fans, and would intentionally avoid them to avoid getting cold shoulders while shopping. Whenever the Dragons lost, Coach Hsu would be lectured on his tactics by street vendors while accompanying his wife to the market the next day. It seems the " armchair manager" existed even back then . In July of that same year, Dragons submarine pitcher Yang Chieh-jen threw the first no-hitter in CPBL history against the San-Hoo, using his deceptive pitches to stymie them and earning the. nickname "Tiger-Slaying Hero." After that season ended, everyone’s attention turned to the future of Japanese-league star Lu Ming-tzu. He joined the Yomiuri Giants in 1988, hitting a home run in his first at-bat in the majors, immediately becoming known as the " Asian Great Cannon" and a household name in Taiwan, though his later career didn't go as expected and he struggled with the Giants. In 1991, he decided to return to Taiwan to play professional baseball, specifically wanting to return to his old team from the Wei-Chuan era. The problem was that the Chinese Professional Baseball League had a draft system. If Lu Ming-Tzu wanted to join a CPBL team, he had to follow the rules and enter the draft, and it was the Brothers who held the first overall pick. that year. In order to secure this " Asian slugger," the Wei-Chuan Dragons decided to make the first move, signing Lu to a hitting coach contract with a monthly salary of 200,000, hoping to get a head start. The other three teams were , of course, unhappy about this. The Brothers even threatened to cancel all upcoming "Dragons vs. Brothers" games, refusing to play against Wei-Chuan on the same field. After much negotiation, Lu Ming-Tzu ultimately had to enter the draft, and as expected, he was selected by the Brothers who held the top pick, even though he still preferred to join the Dragons. This stalemate was finally broken when the Dragons' stolen base king, Lin Yi-Tseng, volunteered to be traded to the Brothers, allowing Lu Ming-Tzu to fulfill his wish and wear. the Dragons 'jersey. And so, before the 1992 spring training, the Dragons traded Lin Yi-Tseng and catcher Chen Yen-Cheng to acquire Lu Ming-Tzu, marking the first player trade in the history of the league. Everyone knows what happened next: Lin Yi-Tseng went to the Brothers , experienced their three-peat, and after retiring, became a manager and led them to another three-peat. As for Lu Ming-Tzu, he did not quite live up to the "slugger" hype everyone expected. Entering the mid-90s, the off-field drama of the Wei-Chuan Dragons was even more theatrical than the games on the field! On the field, the Brother Elephants won three consecutive titles from 1992 to 1994, and the league expanded to six teams in 1993. The " Dragons vs. Brothers" rivalry remained the biggest draw in the league, but the Dragons' performance didn't show much improvement, and they could never beat the Brothers 'submarine pitcher, Chen Hsien-Chang. For 505 days, they couldn't get a single win against him, and Chen earned the nickname "Dragonslayer." As for the off-field situation, we must return to the Wei-Chuan brothers we mentioned earlier and asked you to remember. In 1986, Wei-Chuan founder Huang Lieh-ho handed the business over to his half-brothers: the elder Huang Ke-ming as Chairman and the second son Huang Nan-tu as General Manager. It looked like a standard family succession , but because their personalities were polar opposites—one conservative and one. aggressive—they struggled to reconcile their decision-making, leading to nine years of unhappy coexistence. By 1995, Huang Nan-tu teamed up with market investors to force his older brother out and take over as chairman, but this was akin to inviting outsiders into the family, leading to increasingly diluted family shareholding. Starting in 1996, Wei Chuan fell into consecutive years of losses. As the company hit hard times, the players were the first to feel the impact. In early 1996, the Wei Chuan Dragons adjusted salaries, with an average team increase of only 8%. Some veterans even faced pay cuts, earning less than incoming rookies. Key players like Tseng Chih-mao, Lo Shih-hsin, and.

Yang Chieh-jen went to the Wei Chuan building on Songjiang Road to confront the management. Chairman Chen Chin-kuang simply replied with a Taiwanese idiom, implying that once the company made money, everyone would naturally get a share—though not everyone would get to share in it. At that time, pitcher Lin Guang-hung directly asked for his release from the Dragons. He admitted that another professional league currently in formation had already approached him, and the "other league" he referred to was the Taiwan Major League, founded by Chiu Fu-sheng of the Era Group. In September 1996, they announced an investment of 200 million NT dollars to sign a group of stars from CPBL teams like Wei Chuan and. Uni-President. In December of the same year, five Wei Chuan stars—Huang Ping-yang, Kuo Chien-lin, Sun Chao-li, Li An-hsi, and Kaiser—officially announced they were jumping ship to the Taiwan Major League. Lu Ming-tzu also left Wei Chuan during this wave. According to reports from netizens, Liang Kung-pin, a key figure in the Taiwan Major League at the time, revealed on his podcast that even before the match-fixing scandal, the Wei Chuan management had already lost interest in the team, and with poor compensation, it was no wonder their stars were so easily poached. Of course, some fans argued that Huang Nan-tu had at least publicly promised to continue operations, and the players who stayed the following year. actually received significant raises, but the real storm was yet to come. In early 1997, prosecutors questioned several China Times Eagles players, triggering the Black Eagles match-fixing scandal. At the same time, the Taiwan Major League officially began. A small Taiwan was suddenly packed with 11 professional teams, two leagues, and two sets of schedules. Coupled with frequent rumors of game-throwing, fans would constantly have a question in their minds when entering the stadium: Is this game actually real? It was at this moment that the stands began to empty, marking the official entry into a dark era. And yet, the Wei Chuan Dragons dynasty happened to be right in the middle of this professional baseball. winter. In 1996, the Wei Chuan Dragons’ roster began a generational transition. The team signed 19-year-old trainee Chang Tai-shan through a special tryout . He won the Rookie of the Year award right away and was dubbed the "Prince of the Forest." Yeh Chun-chang, who would later become their star catcher, also joined that same year. The Dragons won the second-half season title, but after reaching the Taiwan Series, they once again returned home empty-handed. In 1997, the Dragons surged in the second half of the season, relying on several powerful foreign players to clinch the second-half title. In the Taiwan Series , they faced the Chinatrust Whales, a team that had just survived the Black Eagles scandal where most of their players were implicated and replaced by loaners from other teams. From the third. game on, the Dragons staged a comeback, winning four consecutive games and securing the championship in Tainan. During those years, the Dragons had the former league batting champion Chen Chin-mao, foreign player Dardo who stole 71 bases in a single season, and the dominant closer Garcia, who pitched 45 consecutive scoreless innings. With the maturation of players like Chang Tai-shan and Yeh Chun-chang, the cards in the manager's hands were getting better and better. However, just as the Dragons' performance began to improve, an "extra-innings" battle was simultaneously unfolding in the business world inside the Wei Chuan building on Songjiang Road. By mid-1997, the market-based investors 'stake in Wei Chuan exceeded 20 percent. Huang Nan-tu. realized something was wrong and rushed to boost the family's stake back to 35 percent. He suggested his father buy more shares, but the 88-year-old Huang Lieh-ho believed the market investors couldn't possibly acquire a majority stake, so he decided not to increase their position. This move turned out to be a critical miscalculation. By the end of the year, other members of the Huang family and the Su family, taking advantage of Huang Nan-tu being abroad, offloaded nearly 10 percent of their shares at a price of around 48 NT dollars, hoping to suppress the market investors by flooding the market. Instead, all these shares were swallowed up by the market investors. In early 1998, stock market operator "Ah Ding," holding nearly 40 percent of the shares , confronted Huang Lieh-ho and demanded. the Huang family buy them back at a high price, but Huang Lieh-ho refused. He was betting that no one in Taiwan would be willing to pay that much for Wei Chuan, and that if the market investors were saddled with heavy interest payments, they would eventually collapse. Little did he expect that someone would strike from across the strait. The Wei family of Yongjing, Changhua—who made their fortune in China with Master Kong instant noodles—the Ting Hsin International Group, led by the four brothers Wei Ying-chou, Wei Ying-chiao, Wei Ying-chung, and Wei Ying-heng, stepped in and bought out the market investors' entire stake at a price even higher than what Ah Ding had demanded. Ting Hsin eventually secured more than half of the board seats, gaining actual control over Wei Chuan. Originally, Ting Hsin intended to keep Huang Nan-tu as. chairman, but the Huang family vetoed it themselves, even removing him from the family's list of directors. Just like that, Wei Chuan, which Huang Lieh-huo had founded and managed for 45 years, officially transitioned from a family business of the Huangs to the Wei family . It is said that when the news was announced, 89-year-old Huang Lieh-huo was devastated for a long time, even wanting to buy Wei Chuan back at any cost, but unfortunately, there were no " what-ifs"—a momentary mistake led to eternal regret. That year, Wei Chuan only ranked third in the regular season , relying on the playoffs to defeat Uni-President and squeeze into the championship series. In the finals, their opponent was the Sinon Bulls, anchored by a powerful lineup of sluggers. However, thanks to pitching.

coach Yang Chieh-jen’s strategies, they neutralized Sinon's power hitters and successfully won the championship, completing a back-to-back title run. But off the field, Wei Chuan wasn't as lucky ; in the second half of 1998, Wei Chuan's stock price plummeted. According to reports from that time, the holdings of the Su and Huang families had dropped to less than 2%, as they prepared to pull out of Wei Chuan entirely. Regardless, entering 1999, Wei Chuan had effectively become a company belonging to the Ting Hsin Group. 1999 began with turmoil. On April 18, Hsu Sheng-ming became the league’s first manager to reach 300 wins, but eight days later, he was stabbed by thugs in. front of his home, becoming the first manager in the league to be injured due to mafia intimidation. On September 20, a game between the Sinon Bulls and the Wei Chuan Dragons drew only 101 spectators. There were more birds in the stands than people, setting a record for the lowest attendance in professional baseball history. Just hours after this game filled with birds ended, the 921 earthquake struck. This natural disaster dealt another heavy blow to an already struggling professional baseball environment. Amid this cold winter for pro baseball, Wei Chuan made it to the championship series again against the Mercuries Tigers, but the series turned out to be unusually heated. In Game 1,. Wei Chuan slugger Ta-ti-shih collided with Mercuries catcher Wang Kuang-hui at home plate. The two got into an argument and a fight broke out. After things finally calmed down, a second brawl erupted in the ninth inning. This incident made the Dragons-Tigers series the most violent championship series in history. This brawl brought the championship series to a climax, as the Wei Chuan Dragons ultimately defeated the Mercuries Tigers four games to one, successfully completing their three-peat dynasty. But very quickly, the high tide was immediately followed by a low ebb. Just one day before the Dragons won the title, the Tigers had already announced their disbandment, and the future of the Dragons, whose parent company was also. suffering heavy losses, remained uncertain. That very night, Hsu Sheng-ming pleaded with the team organization, "You absolutely cannot disband the team!" They then proceeded as planned on their championship trip to Europe, but they were unaware that internally, Wei Chuan had already reached its verdict. According to reports at the time, the Dragons were losing 80 to 90 million a year, and Wei Chuan Corporation had lost over a billion in just the first three quarters of 1999, with stock prices plummeting below 10 dollars, turning into " dumpling stock." Disbanding the team had long been the internal consensus; reports even suggested that if they hadn't won the championship this year, the announcement would have come during the season. On October 30th, just three. weeks after their three-peat, the Wei Chuan Dragons announced a one-year hiatus. The organization emphasized this wasn't a disbandment, claiming coaches and players would still receive 60%of their salaries and the team would return to the CPBL once the environment improved. However, the CPBL naturally did not accept such a vague suspension and demanded that Wei Chuan clearly state whether they were playing or not. When the word "disbandment" finally came up, the fans were heartbroken and began organizing online. On December 12th, a group calling itself the "Save the Dragons" association launched a protest march, calling not just for the team to stay, but for a clean professional league and improvements to the draft. system and stadium facilities. This was the first time in Taiwan's professional baseball history that fans took to the streets for a team, but what was on the mind of Wei Chuan's new boss, Wei Ying-hsing? According to reports, after winning the title, he heard someone say : "The Dragons only won the championship because others threw the games for them ." It was this very sentence that deeply wounded Wei Ying-hsing’s heart. He asked , "Why should I spend money to run a casino for people to gamble?" Organized crime, drugs, and game-fixing—these dark clouds hanging overhead became a major reason for Wei Ying-hsing to disband the team. Sure enough, the next morning on December 13th, the Wei family called team leader Ren Zhongjie to a meeting. and made the final decision to disband. Ren held a press conference that afternoon to announce the sad news. Manager Hsu Sheng-ming, who led the team to a three-peat, was in disbelief and said this to the camera. " >> Hmm, when we won the championship, those were tears of victory. These are truly tears of regret. Honestly, so I just said something that might not sound very comfortable to the Wei family, but I still have to say it.""We left the Huang family only to come to the Wei family, and that’s when we realized the Huang family was actually much better. It sounds harsh, but I still have to say it ." >> At the dissolution press conference that afternoon, the scene was nearly chaotic ! Fans wrote on a whiteboard: "Wei Chuan. is deceiving fans 'feelings; boycott Wei Chuan products." Some people tore up posters and stomped on them, while others sobbed by the door. Some fans asked directly, "If there are financial problems, just be honest. Why blame the professional baseball environment?" Someone even asked the most stinging question: "Why? Was the three-peat real or fake?"" >> So, you cannot ask me whether it was real or fake." "You have to ask the teams that played against us or look at the games throughout the season to see if they were real or not." At that time, some players still hoped that the Farglory Group, or even their old owners, the Huang family and the Su family of Hotai.

, would step in to take over. But in the end, no one showed up. The Dragons had to go their separate ways; Yeh Chun-chang and Chang Tai-shan later transferred to the Sinon Bulls. The CPBL shrunk from six teams back to its original four. Ultimately, who exactly killed the Wei Chuan Dragons? Public criticism of the Wei family was direct: they spent a fortune to buy the Wei Chuan company, only to make the team vanish into thin air at its absolute peak with a single decision. Many loyal fans decided from that day on that they would never buy Wei Chuan products again . However, another group of fans believes that the Huang family was actually the original culprit. Their reasoning is that during the later period of Huang's management, the team had long been neglected. Huang Ping-yang. was even asked to take a pay cut after his surgery. When the A-League (Naruwan ) stepped in, they poached a large number of key players. Losing management rights and selling off shares only made their financial situation worse. When the team disbanded, players waited desperately for their old owners to return, but the Huangs and the Sus never made a move. Some even believe that Hsu Sheng-ming's famous quote was originally meant to complain about the Huang family , only to find that the Wei family was even more disappointing. From my perspective, both arguments hold some truth, but neither tells the whole story . With the league split, the 921 earthquake, and the financial crisis, Taiwanese professional baseball back then was essentially in ruins. Internal. conflicts laid the groundwork, the Wei family made the final decision, and the broader environment pushed the team toward collapse. How did the fans—who had lost their team—spend those 20 years ? After the team disbanded, the official site and forums stopped updating, so the fans taught themselves to build a site from scratch, creating a place called the "Dragon League" to give dispersed fans a home. In an era before social media, this group held gatherings and year-end parties; whenever the veterans played, whether it was Chang Tai-shan or Yeh Chun-chang, a sea of red would always appear in the stands. At the end. of 2018, the last original Wei Chuan Dragon player, Chang Tai-shan, retired, and many thought the name "Wei Chuan Dragons" would remain a memory forever— until, in early 2019, exclusive news broke: the Dragons, missing for 20 years , were officially returning! And the ones behind this revival were none other than the Ting Hsin Wei family, the very ones who had dealt the final blow to the team years ago. In fact, around 2013, the CPBL commissioner at the time, Huang Cheng-tai, had met with Ting Hsin’s Wei Ying-chun, and they had reached a tacit agreement on the team's return, but from late 2013, Ting Hsin became embroiled in. food safety scandals, triggering a boycott in 2014; Wei Chuan’s products took the brunt of it, Wei Ying-chun himself was imprisoned, the brand was effectively dead, and the revival plan was naturally shelved. It wasn't until early 2019 that the plan was finally restarted; as soon as the news broke, people online began saying, "Ting Hsin is buying an indulgence this time." So-called "indulgences" were certificates sold by the medieval church to believers, claimed to offset one’s sins. The fans' meaning was clear: Ting Hsin, whose image hit rock bottom after the food safety scandals, wanted to use baseball to whitewash their reputation. However, some fans were more open-minded , thinking that even if it is an indulgence, as long as it truly helps Taiwanese baseball, then let them buy it . This indulgence certainly isn't cheap ; just the franchise fee is 120 million , plus a 360 million deposit, and another 100 million for the baseball revitalization plan. According to weekly reports, Wei Ying-chun of the Wei family , to reorganize the Wei Chuan Dragons, specially visited Hsu Sheng-ming's widow , Hsieh Jung-yao, who said that before the manager passed, he had said, "If the Dragons ever want to reorganize, I will support it, for the sake of the many kids playing at the grassroots level." The regrets of those years and the remorse of that time seem to have been. put to rest. In May 2019, the CPBL approved the Wei Chuan Dragons ' franchise application, ending the 11- year era of having only four teams. The Dragons drafted 32 rising stars in one go; the top pick was Liu Chi-hung, with a 5.9 million signing bonus, who was dubbed the "Little Chang Tai-shan" and set a record for position players, while their second pick was the future fireballer, Hsu Jo-hsi. The coaching staff was anchored by veteran Dragons who achieved the "three-peat" back in the day, such as Yeh Chun-chang, Chang Tai-shan, and Huang Yang-lung. In 2021, the Dragons returned to the major league , making Tianmu Baseball Stadium their home field. To bolster their roster, they signed former MLB pitcher Wang Wei-chung to a five-year contract worth over 60 million, making him the bona. fide "Dragon King." At the draft the following year, they also added the slugger Giljegiljaw Kungkuan. After three years of team building, they finally succeeded in winning a half-season title and the best overall winning percentage in 2023, returning to the Taiwan Series for the first time in 24 years. Behind ace pitcher Hsu Jo-hsi’s stellar performance, the Wei Chuan Dragons tied the series against the Rakuten Monkeys in Game 6, and in the do-or-die Game 7, they successfully defeated their opponents, showering the field in long-awaited red streamers. At this moment, 20 years of bitterness and waiting transformed into the joy of victory. Manager Yeh Chun-chang also wept, saying, "Because it’s the Dragons , many past memories flooded my mind, so.

it feels very different." It is precisely because the Dragons won the championship that those 20 years of regrets experienced by the fans could finally be truly put to rest. Returning to this year's Taiwan Series, the Wei Chuan Dragons relied on their three strong foreign pitchers to lock down the situation early, taking a 3-1 lead in the series. Unexpectedly, a typhoon gave the CTBC Brothers a chance to recover. They flipped the script in both Game 4 and Game 5, making a "come back from 1-3 to win 4-3" scenario seem very likely. However, in Game 6, foreign pitcher Mercedes completely shut down the Brothers' lineup, eventually sealing the win and securing their second championship trophy since their return to the league. However, the championship. champagne hadn’t even dried yet when Wei Chuan Dragons owner Wei Ying-chun said during a celebratory livestream that they lost Games 4 and 5 simply to give the Brothers a chance and some hope in the "Dragon-Elephant War." He even claimed that every game at the Taipei Dome was a sell-out of 40,000 fans, so he had to thank manager Yeh Chun-chang for his meticulous planning. Not to mention the new fans who didn’t find the owner’s joke funny, the old-school fans who know the history of the Wei Chuan Dragons were absolutely livid. Twenty-seven years ago, Wei Ying-hsing disbanded the team out of heartbreak after hearing people say their championship wasn't earned but gifted to them by others. Twenty-seven years later. , a member of the Wei family turned those same accusations—letting the opponent win and "meticulous planning"— into a joke at a victory banquet, casting a shadow over a championship the players fought six games to win. This one comment has made many people reflect on whether this current iteration of the Dragons is now fundamentally different from the "Royal" Dragons of the past. Personally, I feel the most unique thing about Wei Chuan isn't their three-and-a-half-year turnaround or the two titles since their revival, but those 20 years when the team didn't exist, yet the fans never left. I still remember those years before the Dragons returned; every time I saw a Wei Chuan. Dragons flag, regardless of the time or place, I knew these fans were still there. Even though the players left the field, they never gave up, waiting until the team name finally appeared in the CPBL matchups once again. It was only because this group held the fort that when the team reformed 20 years later, a whole generation of old fans and players were willing to return. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 從味全龍奪冠重返榮耀的畫面出發，回顧龍象對決的經典與遺憾。
  • 梳理味全企業的家族背景與球隊興衰，理解商業決策如何改變一支球隊的命運。
  • 重現黃平洋在總冠軍賽中的驚人表現，感受台灣職棒初期的拚戰精神與代價。

摘要

龍象首度在冠軍賽交鋒，味全龍重返榮耀

作者以2026年台灣大賽第六戰開場：味全龍在第八局由捕手蔣宏擊出全壘打，最終以四勝二敗擊敗中信兄弟，奪下總冠軍。這是中職史上首次由「龍象」兩支元老球隊在總冠軍賽交手，也讓球迷再次想起味全龍的興衰與重生。

作者回顧，味全龍曾在1990年代與兄弟象形成經典對抗，卻在強盛之際遭到解散。1999年，味全企業以職棒簽賭風波為由停掉球隊，魏家接手後更正式解散球隊；但球迷也知道，食品事業虧損與職棒票房前景不佳，才是球隊走入歷史的重要背景。當年數千名龍迷冒著寒風上街抗議，成為台灣職棒史上首次球迷為球隊發起的遊行。二十年後，魏家又讓味全龍重返球場，使球迷不禁思索：今日的紅色，是否仍等同於記憶中的味全龍？

味全企業的家族根源與棒球緣起

故事回到企業創辦人黃烈火。1939年，他在日本神戶創立合泰商會，戰後將事業帶回台灣並取得豐田代理權，發展為和泰汽車；1953年，他成立生產味精的公司，隔年改名為味全。味全食品從味精拓展至醬油、罐頭、奶粉與果汁，成為台灣第一家上市食品公司，曾與統一分據市場南北。

黃家與蘇家共同經營和泰、味全等事業，家族版圖涵蓋汽車、食品、房地產與金融。然而，黃烈火兩房所生的長子黃克銘與黃南圖年齡相差十餘歲、關係疏遠，而兩人的家族脈絡也與味全龍的命運緊密相連。1978年，台中宜寧高中棒球隊因經費不足面臨解散，味全原本只打算資助一學期，球隊卻接連奪下全國冠軍與世界青棒賽冠軍，促使味全進一步投入青棒，並與文化大學合作培育成棒隊伍。

紅軍登場與職棒初代霸業

1988年中華職棒籌組期間，味全積極布局，不只計畫在埔頂牧場興建球場，也招攬海外球員與業餘名將黃平洋。1990年職棒正式開打，身穿紅衣的「紅軍」味全龍登上職棒舞台。當年四月的龍象戰吸引一萬六千名觀眾，創下聯盟首次滿場紀錄，從此成為票房保證。

味全龍首季由黃平洋、洋投史提夫・翁提維洛斯與性格火爆的荷西・紐內茲組成投手「三本柱」，三人合計拿下球隊52勝中的46勝。龍隊在總冠軍賽迎戰兄弟象，黃平洋於第六戰完投完封，助球隊以四勝二敗奪得中職史上第一座總冠軍，也點燃台灣職棒熱潮。

黃平洋的連戰紀錄與極限考驗

作者特別介紹被稱為「金臂人」的黃平洋。他擅長多種變化球，因球路繁多而有「七彩變化球」之稱；加入味全首年便身兼先發與後援，投出246局、拿下20勝，工作量遠超現代職棒常態。

1991年總冠軍賽，味全龍與統一獅展開勢均力敵的「食品大戰」。黃平洋第一戰投131球完投勝，休息三天後又在第四戰投滿14局、用球182顆，雖遭再見安打仍繼續扛起重任。第六戰他再度登板，以130球完封、僅被敲三支安打，將系列賽逼進第七戰；不到24小時後，先發投手提早退場，他又上場救援。耗盡體力的黃平洋最終遭統一獅擊出11支安打，這段賽事既凸顯他的傳奇，也呈現當年投手承受的沉重負荷。

With the second generation of the Huangs adding construction, leasing, and securities, their business empire covered automotive , food, real estate, and finance. Calling the Huang family a prestigious. business dynasty in Taiwan is no exaggeration at all. However, this prestigious family had turbulent undercurrents. other companies that expressed interest included Uni-President, Evergreen, and Wei-Chuan. As. the second-half champions of the inaugural season, the Dragons faced the Brother Elephants in the Taiwan Series. Huang Ping-yang pitched a nine-inning shutout in Game 6, and the Dragons ultimately won 4-2 to claim the first championship trophy in CPBL history, igniting the professional baseball craze in Taiwan. At this point, we must talk more about this "Golden Arm" Huang Ping-yang. Expert in various breaking pitches, he had so many types that he was nicknamed the "Seven-Colored Breaking Ball." What truly turned Huang Ping-yang into a legend was the following year, the 1991 championship series. That year featured a "food war" between the Taipei-based Weichuan Dragons and the Southern powerhouse Uni-President Lions. Both teams had an identical record of 46 wins that season, showing how evenly matched their strength was. Major League along with several teammates. At this point, his speed was gone and his performance wasn't what it used to be, but he was still in Taiwan. Key players like Tseng Chih-mao, Lo Shih-hsin, and.

Yang Chieh-jen went to the Wei Chuan building on Songjiang Road to confront the management. A small Taiwan was suddenly packed with 11 professional teams, two leagues, and two sets of schedules. Coupled with frequent rumors of game-throwing, fans would constantly have a question in their minds when entering the stadium: Is this game actually real? It was at this moment that the stands began to empty, marking the official entry into a dark era. And yet, the Wei Chuan Dragons dynasty happened to be right in the middle of this professional baseball. winter. In 1996, the Wei Chuan Dragons’ roster began a generational transition. The team signed 19-year-old trainee Chang Tai-shan through a special tryout . He won the Rookie of the Year award right away and was dubbed the "Prince of the Forest." Yeh Chun-chang, who would later become their star catcher, also joined that same year. The Dragons won the second-half season title, but after reaching the Taiwan Series, they once again returned home empty-handed. In 1997, the Dragons surged in the second half of the season, relying on several powerful foreign players to clinch the second-half title. In the Taiwan Series , they faced the Chinatrust Whales, a team that had just survived the Black Eagles scandal where most of their players were implicated and replaced by loaners from other teams. From the third. game on, the Dragons staged a comeback, winning four consecutive games and securing the championship in Tainan. During those years, the Dragons had the former league batting champion Chen Chin-mao, foreign player Dardo who stole 71 bases in a single season, and the dominant closer Garcia, who pitched 45 consecutive scoreless innings. With the maturation of players like Chang Tai-shan and Yeh Chun-chang, the cards in the manager's hands were getting better and better. However, just as the Dragons' performance began to improve, an "extra-innings" battle was simultaneously unfolding in the business world inside the Wei Chuan building on Songjiang Road. By mid-1997, the market-based investors 'stake in Wei Chuan exceeded 20 percent. Huang Nan-tu. realized something was wrong and rushed to boost the family's stake back to 35 percent. He suggested his father buy more shares, but the 88-year-old Huang Lieh-ho believed the market investors couldn't possibly acquire a majority stake, so he decided not to increase their position. This move turned out to be a critical miscalculation. By the end of the year, other members of the Huang family and the Su family, taking advantage of Huang Nan-tu being abroad, offloaded nearly 10 percent of their shares at a price of around 48 NT dollars, hoping to suppress the market investors by flooding the market. Instead, all these shares were swallowed up by the market investors. In early 1998, stock market operator "Ah Ding," holding nearly 40 percent of the shares , confronted Huang Lieh-ho and demanded. the Huang family buy them back at a high price, but Huang Lieh-ho refused. He was betting that no one in Taiwan would be willing to pay that much for Wei Chuan, and that if the market investors were saddled with heavy interest payments, they would eventually collapse. Little did he expect that someone would strike from across the strait. The Wei family of Yongjing, Changhua—who made their fortune in China with Master Kong instant noodles—the Ting Hsin International Group, led by the four brothers Wei Ying-chou, Wei Ying-chiao, Wei Ying-chung, and Wei Ying-heng, stepped in and bought out the market investors' entire stake at a price even higher than what Ah Ding had demanded. Ting Hsin eventually secured more than half of the board seats, gaining actual control over Wei Chuan. Originally, Ting Hsin intended to keep Huang Nan-tu as. chairman, but the Huang family vetoed it themselves, even removing him from the family's list of directors. Just like that, Wei Chuan, which Huang Lieh-huo had founded and managed for 45 years, officially transitioned from a family business of the Huangs to the Wei family . It is said that when the news was announced, 89-year-old Huang Lieh-huo was devastated for a long time, even wanting to buy Wei Chuan back at any cost, but unfortunately, there were no " what-ifs"—a momentary mistake led to eternal regret. That year, Wei Chuan only ranked third in the regular season , relying on the playoffs to defeat Uni-President and squeeze into the championship series. In the finals, their opponent was the Sinon Bulls, anchored by a powerful lineup of sluggers. However, thanks to pitching.

coach Yang Chieh-jen’s strategies, they neutralized Sinon's power hitters and successfully won the championship, completing a back-to-back title run. But off the field, Wei Chuan wasn't as lucky ; in the second half of 1998, Wei Chuan's stock price plummeted. According to reports from that time, the holdings of the Su and Huang families had dropped to less than 2%, as they prepared to pull out of Wei Chuan entirely. Regardless, entering 1999, Wei Chuan had effectively become a company belonging to the Ting Hsin Group. 1999 began with turmoil. On April 18, Hsu Sheng-ming became the league’s first manager to reach 300 wins, but eight days later, he was stabbed by thugs in. front of his home, becoming the first manager in the league to be injured due to mafia intimidation. On September 20, a game between the Sinon Bulls and the Wei Chuan Dragons drew only 101 spectators. There were more birds in the stands than people, setting a record for the lowest attendance in professional baseball history. Just hours after this game filled with birds ended, the 921 earthquake struck. This natural disaster dealt another heavy blow to an already struggling professional baseball environment. Amid this cold winter for pro baseball, Wei Chuan made it to the championship series again against the Mercuries Tigers, but the series turned out to be unusually heated. In Game 1,. Wei Chuan slugger Ta-ti-shih collided with Mercuries catcher Wang Kuang-hui at home plate. The two got into an argument and a fight broke out. After things finally calmed down, a second brawl erupted in the ninth inning. This incident made the Dragons-Tigers series the most violent championship series in history. This brawl brought the championship series to a climax, as the Wei Chuan Dragons ultimately defeated the Mercuries Tigers four games to one, successfully completing their three-peat dynasty. But very quickly, the high tide was immediately followed by a low ebb. Just one day before the Dragons won the title, the Tigers had already announced their disbandment, and the future of the Dragons, whose parent company was also. suffering heavy losses, remained uncertain. That very night, Hsu Sheng-ming pleaded with the team organization, "You absolutely cannot disband the team!" They then proceeded as planned on their championship trip to Europe, but they were unaware that internally, Wei Chuan had already reached its verdict. According to reports at the time, the Dragons were losing 80 to 90 million a year, and Wei Chuan Corporation had lost over a billion in just the first three quarters of 1999, with stock prices plummeting below 10 dollars, turning into " dumpling stock." Disbanding the team had long been the internal consensus; reports even suggested that if they hadn't won the championship this year, the announcement would have come during the season. On October 30th, just three. weeks after their three-peat, the Wei Chuan Dragons announced a one-year hiatus. The organization emphasized this wasn't a disbandment, claiming coaches and players would still receive 60%of their salaries and the team would return to the CPBL once the environment improved. However, the CPBL naturally did not accept such a vague suspension and demanded that Wei Chuan clearly state whether they were playing or not. When the word "disbandment" finally came up, the fans were heartbroken and began organizing online. On December 12th, a group calling itself the "Save the Dragons" association launched a protest march, calling not just for the team to stay, but for a clean professional league and improvements to the draft. system and stadium facilities. This was the first time in Taiwan's professional baseball history that fans took to the streets for a team, but what was on the mind of Wei Chuan's new boss, Wei Ying-hsing? According to reports, after winning the title, he heard someone say : "The Dragons only won the championship because others threw the games for them ." It was this very sentence that deeply wounded Wei Ying-hsing’s heart. He asked , "Why should I spend money to run a casino for people to gamble?" Organized crime, drugs, and game-fixing—these dark clouds hanging overhead became a major reason for Wei Ying-hsing to disband the team. Sure enough, the next morning on December 13th, the Wei family called team leader Ren Zhongjie to a meeting. and made the final decision to disband. Ren held a press conference that afternoon to announce the sad news. Manager Hsu Sheng-ming, who led the team to a three-peat, was in disbelief and said this to the camera. " >> Hmm, when we won the championship, those were tears of victory. These are truly tears of regret. Honestly, so I just said something that might not sound very comfortable to the Wei family, but I still have to say it.""We left the Huang family only to come to the Wei family, and that’s when we realized the Huang family was actually much better. It sounds harsh, but I still have to say it ." >> At the dissolution press conference that afternoon, the scene was nearly chaotic ! Fans wrote on a whiteboard: "Wei Chuan. is deceiving fans 'feelings; boycott Wei Chuan products." Some people tore up posters and stomped on them, while others sobbed by the door. Some fans asked directly, "If there are financial problems, just be honest. Why blame the professional baseball environment?" Someone even asked the most stinging question: "Why? Was the three-peat real or fake?"" >> So, you cannot ask me whether it was real or fake." "You have to ask the teams that played against us or look at the games throughout the season to see if they were real or not." At that time, some players still hoped that the Farglory Group, or even their old owners, the Huang family and the Su family of Hotai.

, would step in to take over. But in the end, no one showed up. The Dragons had to go their separate ways; Yeh Chun-chang and Chang Tai-shan later transferred to the Sinon Bulls. The CPBL shrunk from six teams back to its original four. Ultimately, who exactly killed the Wei Chuan Dragons? Public criticism of the Wei family was direct: they spent a fortune to buy the Wei Chuan company, only to make the team vanish into thin air at its absolute peak with a single decision. Many loyal fans decided from that day on that they would never buy Wei Chuan products again . However, another group of fans believes that the Huang family was actually the original culprit. Their reasoning is that during the later period of Huang's management, the team had long been neglected. Huang Ping-yang. was even asked to take a pay cut after his surgery. When the A-League (Naruwan ) stepped in, they poached a large number of key players. Losing management rights and selling off shares only made their financial situation worse. When the team disbanded, players waited desperately for their old owners to return, but the Huangs and the Sus never made a move. Some even believe that Hsu Sheng-ming's famous quote was originally meant to complain about the Huang family , only to find that the Wei family was even more disappointing. From my perspective, both arguments hold some truth, but neither tells the whole story . With the league split, the 921 earthquake, and the financial crisis, Taiwanese professional baseball back then was essentially in ruins. Internal. conflicts laid the groundwork, the Wei family made the final decision, and the broader environment pushed the team toward collapse. How did the fans—who had lost their team—spend those 20 years ? After the team disbanded, the official site and forums stopped updating, so the fans taught themselves to build a site from scratch, creating a place called the "Dragon League" to give dispersed fans a home. In an era before social media, this group held gatherings and year-end parties; whenever the veterans played, whether it was Chang Tai-shan or Yeh Chun-chang, a sea of red would always appear in the stands. At the end. of 2018, the last original Wei Chuan Dragon player, Chang Tai-shan, retired, and many thought the name "Wei Chuan Dragons" would remain a memory forever— until, in early 2019, exclusive news broke: the Dragons, missing for 20 years , were officially returning! And the ones behind this revival were none other than the Ting Hsin Wei family, the very ones who had dealt the final blow to the team years ago. In fact, around 2013, the CPBL commissioner at the time, Huang Cheng-tai, had met with Ting Hsin’s Wei Ying-chun, and they had reached a tacit agreement on the team's return, but from late 2013, Ting Hsin became embroiled in. food safety scandals, triggering a boycott in 2014; Wei Chuan’s products took the brunt of it, Wei Ying-chun himself was imprisoned, the brand was effectively dead, and the revival plan was naturally shelved. It wasn't until early 2019 that the plan was finally restarted; as soon as the news broke, people online began saying, "Ting Hsin is buying an indulgence this time." So-called "indulgences" were certificates sold by the medieval church to believers, claimed to offset one’s sins. The fans' meaning was clear: Ting Hsin, whose image hit rock bottom after the food safety scandals, wanted to use baseball to whitewash their reputation. However, some fans were more open-minded , thinking that even if it is an indulgence, as long as it truly helps Taiwanese baseball, then let them buy it . According to weekly reports, Wei Ying-chun of the Wei family , to reorganize the Wei Chuan Dragons, specially visited Hsu Sheng-ming's widow , Hsieh Jung-yao, who said that before the manager passed, he had said, "If the Dragons ever want to reorganize, I will support it, for the sake of the many kids playing at the grassroots level." The regrets of those years and the remorse of that time seem to have been. put to rest. In May 2019, the CPBL approved the Wei Chuan Dragons ' franchise application, ending the 11- year era of having only four teams. The Dragons drafted 32 rising stars in one go; the top pick was Liu Chi-hung, with a 5.9 million signing bonus, who was dubbed the "Little Chang Tai-shan" and set a record for position players, while their second pick was the future fireballer, Hsu Jo-hsi. The coaching staff was anchored by veteran Dragons who achieved the "three-peat" back in the day, such as Yeh Chun-chang, Chang Tai-shan, and Huang Yang-lung. In 2021, the Dragons returned to the major league , making Tianmu Baseball Stadium their home field. To bolster their roster, they signed former MLB pitcher Wang Wei-chung to a five-year contract worth over 60 million, making him the bona. fide "Dragon King." At the draft the following year, they also added the slugger Giljegiljaw Kungkuan. After three years of team building, they finally succeeded in winning a half-season title and the best overall winning percentage in 2023, returning to the Taiwan Series for the first time in 24 years. Behind ace pitcher Hsu Jo-hsi’s stellar performance, the Wei Chuan Dragons tied the series against the Rakuten Monkeys in Game 6, and in the do-or-die Game 7, they successfully defeated their opponents, showering the field in long-awaited red streamers. At this moment, 20 years of bitterness and waiting transformed into the joy of victory. Manager Yeh Chun-chang also wept, saying, "Because it’s the Dragons , many past memories flooded my mind, so.

it feels very different." It is precisely because the Dragons won the championship that those 20 years of regrets experienced by the fans could finally be truly put to rest. Unexpectedly, a typhoon gave the CTBC Brothers a chance to recover. They flipped the script in both Game 4 and Game 5, making a "come back from 1-3 to win 4-3" scenario seem very likely.
