As Taiwanese athletes broke world records and won gold medals, all of Taiwan was ignited by the passion and excitement on the field; even track and field, usually considered a niche sport in Taiwan, drew packed crowds to the stadium thanks to the stellar performances of athletes like Cheng Chao-tsun. Under the coordination of then-Secretary-General Su Li-chiung, the slogan "We're going home to compete" fully triggered the public's intense interest in the Universiade. After the Universiade, Ko Wen-je’s approval rating soared back to 60%, and an event. originally written off became the crowning achievement of his first term. However, just as Ko Wen-je’s popularity reached its peak, the rift between him and the Green camp grew even deeper. This was because, just over a month before the Universiade, Ko Wen-je had attended the 的 双城 論壇 (Twin City Forum) in Shanghai, where he once again mentioned his "two sides of the strait are one family" rhetoric and added a proposal to build a "cross-strait community with a shared destiny." Although Ko Wen-je claimed this goodwill gesture toward China was to ensure the success of the Universiade, the pan-green grassroots simply could not accept it. To them, the mayor they once staunchly supported had become。increasingly like a stranger. Immediately after the Universiade, the political talk show "Political Shock," hosted by Professor Dennis Peng, extensively covered the controversy over the ban on Taiwanese flags at the event . Although it was later confirmed that the Military Police were in charge of venue security and the Taipei City Government had no authority to command them, rumors persist. Deep-green and pro-independence supporters could not accept Ko's remarks, and Ko's subsequent attacks on the pan-green camp sowed the seeds for the later white-green split. For the Kuomintang, attempting to block. Ko Wen-je's reelection after the Universiade, with his popularity soaring , became an increasingly daunting task. Some in the party hoped that Legislator Chiang Wan-an, who had just turned 40, would run, as he was the only one with a chance to compete with Ko, who held strong support among young people. However, Chiang refused decisively, announcing in January 2018 that he would not run for mayor. With that, the KMT’s heavy baton finally passed to the man who refused to quit for 24 years: Ting Shou-chung. Ting had wanted to run for Taipei mayor since 1994. Over the years. , he lost to Huang Ta-chou, stepped aside for Ma Ying-jeou, and later lost to Hau Lung-bin and Sean Lien; he could be called the symbol of KMT tragedy. After 24 years, and thanks to Chiang Wan-an's refusal to run, he finally won the party primary and was chosen to officially represent the KMT in the 2018 Taipei mayoral election. Although some commentators felt that the KMT had no other options, making Ting the vanguard , his local political strength, built through many consecutive terms as a legislator in Taipei, was definitely not to be underestimated. Unlike Ko Wen-je's advantage in online "air warfare," Ting. Shou-chung relied on the KMT’s traditional "ground" organization and the inherent blue-leaning voter base, which still proved effective. Having discussed the KMT, what about the DPP? Initially, the DPP did consider cooperating with Ko Wen-je again, but the problem was that the voices within the DPP grassroots demanding no more concessions were growing louder. In January 2018, during an interview, President Tsai Ing-wen was asked whether Ko Wen-je was an ally of the DPP. Tsai responded that Ko needed to reaffirm his "Taiwan values" to gain the recognition of DPP supporters. When the phrase " Taiwan values" was thrown out, some believed that Tsai Ing-wen was pushing. the pressure of a green-white coalition back onto Ko Wen-je. After all, in 2014 , to facilitate cooperation, Tsai had shouldered most of the pressure within the party. Instead of backing Ko again, she decided to let him explain his stance to green-camp supporters himself . However, the public held different views on Tsai's introduction of "Taiwan values." Many netizens questioned whether asking people to define their own "Taiwan values" amounted to ideological screening. Phrases like " your Taiwan values are insufficient" or "upholding Taiwan values" began to turn into forms of online mockery. By this time, some in the DPP could no longer sit still. In April, Legislator Yao.

Wen-chih organized a march for his Taipei mayoral bid, calling on thousands to take to the streets. Beyond demonstrating momentum, he aimed to pressure the party headquarters to nominate their own candidate. The event was ultimately defined as an anti-Ko march, where opposing Ko Wen-je and the green-white coalition became the main demands. Facing overwhelming pressure from within the party, the person who made the final decision was Presidential Office Secretary-General Chen Chu. Chen Chu firmly insisted that the DPP should not......continue to accommodate Ko Wen-je. Beyond the fact that grassroots supporters were generally dissatisfied with him, she believed that even if the DPP were to lose, it should uphold the party's own autonomy. She made a very. direct statement: "We can be different from him." After this remark, the relationship between the green camp and the white camp had almost reached its end. Although Ko Wen-je later appeared on Green Peace Radio to apologize to those offended by his "one family on both sides of the strait" remark, this gesture was criticized by the blue camp and rejected by the green camp as well. With that, the split between the white and green camps was officially solidified. The DPP formally nominated Yao Wen-chih for mayor at the end of May . The race returned to...After the DPP confirmed Yao’s nomination, TVBS released figures: Ting Shou-chung at 33. %, Ko Wen-je at 31%, and Yao Wen-chih at 13%, marking the first time Ko had fallen behind. Among DPP supporters, 49 %backed Yao Wen-chih, while only 32% supported Ko Wen-je; the green camp's vote had been starkly split in two. In Ko Wen-je's voter demographic, the younger generation aged 20 to 39 accounted for over 50%of his support, but among seniors over 60, his support dropped to just 11%. Scholars analyze that the controversy over cutting senior welfare payments, combined with his outspoken and gaffe-prone personality, are the biggest factors behind the dissatisfaction among middle-aged and elderly groups toward Ko Wen-je. Now,. without the grassroots organizational support of the DPP, it has become incredibly difficult for Ko Wen-je to reach these voters. Without a political party or an organization, how exactly is Ko Wen-je's team supposed to fight this battle? They have to find a way to secure all their own funding and buzz. First, in 2017, Ko Wen-je filmed a video with a YouTuber to promote the Universiade and became an instant hit! At that point, his aides wondered, if they replicated this approach for promoting municipal affairs, would it be possible to create the same impact? Ko Wen-je's social media team approached Walkgame and proposed a collaboration with their signature program, "The Mayor's Aide." Ultimately, "The Mayor's. Aide" was released in early July, featuring a host following Ko Wen-je for an entire day to experience the hardships of being a political aide. The natural presentation of the program, interspersed with various bits of humor , immediately ignited online traffic. In the first three days, the average daily view count exceeded 1 million, and by August 20th, it officially surpassed 10 million, becoming YouTube's top trending video of 2018. This video almost completely swept away the decline in polls that Ko's camp had experienced in the months following the split between the "White" and "Green" camps. Later, Ko Wen-je's team proposed another collaboration with Joeman for "Joe vs. Challenge," which also hit staggering view counts, and these segments. precisely highlighted the political achievements the Ko administration wanted to promote. In "The Mayor's Aide ," they visited the renovation site of the Huanan Market, and for "Joe vs. Challenge"......they ate lunch boxes in social housing with Joeman, effortlessly and naturally bringing Ko Wen-je's policy achievements to different online platforms. Shortly after "The Mayor's Aide" went online, TVBS released another Taipei mayoral poll; Ko Wen-je jumped from 31%to 40%, a growth of nine percentage points. Ting Shou-chung dropped to 30%, turning his previous narrow lead over Ko into a double-digit deficit, while Yao Wen-chih's poll numbers were at 11%. Even more notably,. young voters flocked back to support Ko Wen-je, with his support rate among those aged 20 to 39 surging to nearly 70 %. Even among those who identify with the DPP, the proportion supporting Ko Wen-je surpassed that of the DPP’s own nominee, Yao Wen-chih, as Ko regained the support of the majority of green-leaning voters. Once momentum picked up, Ko Wen-je's next step was to raise funds. With no support from any political party or foundation, Ko decided to ask his wife......Chen Pei-chi, to take out a 20 million NTD loan against their house, providing the first pot of gold for his election campaign. After receiving the money, his campaign office officially opened in.

July, with his Facebook editor becoming the very first employee. To everyone's surprise, unlike other flashy campaign offices, the staff actually worked out of a co-working space, embracing a minimalist style—or rather, a severely modest one. This image of poverty immediately stirred up sympathy from his supporters. Within just nine hours of the small-sum fundraising website going live, they had raised over 37 million NTD, breaking the records of both Blue and Green political figures. Before the end of summer, Ko Wen-je seemed to be back on track. However, it didn't last long; the "Han Wave" created by KMT. Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Han Kuo-yu began blowing north from Kaohsiung starting in late August. We have already covered the Han Wave in previous episodes, so we won't go into detail here. Han Kuo-yu’s personal charisma and his frequent soundbites directly drove ratings and web traffic, no matter what . Whether it was news praising him or commentary criticizing him, anything related to Han Kuo-yu drew huge audiences. At the time, the two major evening political talk shows, "Critical Moment" and "News Tornado," practically became fan channels for Han because their ratings were so impressive. If one could argue that web traffic might be influenced by China, then traditional TV. ratings should be enough to prove that the Han Wave was real. The person hit hardest by this Han Wave was Ko Wen-je, who was also campaigning that year; desperately needing web traffic and visibility, he was almost completely overshadowed, his media coverage cut in half, and online traffic all centered on Han Kuo-yu. This also fully awakened the previously stagnant Blue camp supporters , and even Ting Shou-chung, who had been mocked for his "Zen-like" campaign, saw his standing rise along with the tide. According to a TVBS poll in mid-September, Ko Wen-je was at 37%and Ting Shou-chung at 32%; the gap between the Blue and White camps shrank from 10 %to just 5 percentage points, proving. that this wave had spillover effects. By October, the Ko Wen-je camp dropped another bombshell, if everyone remembers . As we mentioned in the last episode, Lien Sheng-wen publicly cited the book " The Slaughter," written by an American investigative journalist, during a debate to accuse his opponent, Ko Wen-je , of involvement in organ trafficking in China. Back then, Ko Wen-je produced a lawyer's letter from the author of*The Slaughter*to successfully defeat Sean Lien. Unexpectedly, four years later, the book's author, Dr. Gutmann, arrived in Taiwan to hold an international press conference. This time, however, he pointed his finger at Ko Wen-je,. accusing him of acting as a middleman in China's organ transplant industry and even teaching Chinese doctors how to use ECMO in transplants, labeling Ko as one of the culprits behind live organ harvesting. At the scene, a member of the public asked Gutmann if he considered Ko Wen-je a liar, and he answered directly. Gutmann's personal appearance and his 180-degree shift in stance stunned everyone, especially since his lawyer's letter four years prior had endorsed Ko as a man of moral courage. Ko Wen-je's camp quickly filed a lawsuit against Gutmann and lashed out , calling him an election mercenary. This organ donation storm did not affect. Ko's momentum. According to an October survey by the Taiwan Public Opinion Foundation, only 19%of Taipei citizens agreed with Gutmann's claims, while as many as 60%disagreed. At the time, even Premier Lai Ching-te stepped forward, immediately setting the tone by stating that he believed Ko Wen-je. However, Yao Wen-chih, who was third in the polls, chose to take a gamble by biting directly into the controversy surrounding Ko's organ transplants. He argued that Ko's answers and Gutmann's accusations were at odds, with Ko dodging questions. He said if Ko could publicly condemn the CCP for harvesting organs from Falun Gong practitioners, he would publicly apologize to Ko; otherwise, he would continue to publicly. question the matter. It wasn't just Yao Wen-chih who jumped on the organ transplant controversy; even Ting Shou-chung didn't let it go, demanding that Ko publicly clarify the dispute. DPP elder Lin Cho-shui publicly rebuked Yao Wen-chih, stating that while this radical path might bring deep-green voters back, the cost would be that light-green and independent voters would all drift toward Ko Wen-je. As the story reaches this point, I would like to ask everyone to please subscribe. Subscribing is easy for you and won't affect your YouTube homepage algorithm at all, but for us, the subscription count is the most tangible encouragement and helps us get noticed by sponsors.

One person subscribes, one person is happy; 300,000 subscribers, 300,000 are happy. Let’s grow together. Regarding Ting Shou-chung mentioned earlier, another municipal project he aggressively attacked was the Taipei Dome controversy. After Ko Wen-je took office, the Taipei Dome was ordered to stop construction by the city government due to deviations from the original blueprints, turning it into a massive ruin in the city center. Ting criticized Ko, saying he lacks the guts to tear it down and the nerve to finish it. He claimed that if he were mayor, he could easily resolve the Taipei Dome controversy within two months of taking office. Meanwhile, the Ko Wen-je team chose to face voters directly. On October 11, the campaign launched an online show, "Uncle Face-to-Face," borrowing the popular international car-interview format to invite citizens into a vehicle for a direct conversation with Ko, tackling issues like the Taipei Dome controversy, the cancellation of senior citizen subsidies, and whether Ko is anti-business or anti-wealth, allowing these questions to be asked openly. This approach not only drove traffic but also addressed various outside doubts regarding Ko Wen-je's governance. Speaking of the air war, the most interesting event during this period was a rap battle. On October 7, the Ting Shou-chung camp released a rap campaign song, "Taipei's Future is in Our Hands," using a pun on "Ting" and " in hand." It hit 100,000 views in one day, but was immediately criticized by. producer Hsu Chang-te, who remarked that turning rap into a rhythmic folk rhyme would only hurt their own listeners. The Ting camp remained unfazed, believing that as long as the song was catchy, it achieved its purpose. Three weeks later , Ko Wen-je released his first single, collaborating with hip-hop label Colours and rapper Chun-yen. His catchphrase, " It’s weird," became part of the song, sounding surprisingly like a real rap track. One was mocked as a rhythmic folk rhyme, while the other was dubbed by netizens as a hip-hop superstar delayed by his medical career; the gap between the two sides in the youth battlefield was clear. However, no matter how brilliantly the air war is fought, Ko. Wen-je's greatest enemy remains his own mouth. Again, on October 20, during a youth forum discussing aesthetics, he blurted out that Japanese women always wear makeup before going out, unlike some Taiwanese women who go out in public looking frightening. As soon as he said this, the audience gasped; Ko himself took it lightly, laughing that he had "spoken out of turn" again. Just as one wave subsided, another rose. A week later, on October 27, while speaking with the chairwoman of the National Women's League, Ko said, "The League is operating well now, why care about what they did in the past?" Since the Women's League has long been seen as. a KMT affiliate and part of the party's assets, this remark was viewed by the Pan-Green camp as a denial of transitional justice, turning many of his supporters into critics. Ko’s troubles didn't end there. On November 5 , his campaign director, writer Hsiao Yeh, appeared in a campaign video for Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Chen Chi-mai , publicly endorsing him. As soon as this video was released, it infuriated many light-blue voters who supported both Han Kuo-yu and Ko. They believed Han Kuo-yu treated Ko Wen-je with loyalty, choosing not to come to Taipei to support Ting Shou-chung. Despite. repeated invitations from the Ting camp hoping to bring the "Han Wave" to Taipei , Han declined them all out of gratitude for Ko’s past help. Yet, Ko Wen-je unexpectedly let his own campaign manager film a video endorsing Chen Chi-mai. The outraged comments from Han's supporters nearly flooded Ko’s social media posts. His camp later claimed it was a personal endorsement of Chen Chi-mai and had nothing to do with Ko, but the damage to his polling numbers had already been done. According to mid-November TVBS polling data, Ko Wen-je’s support stood at 39%, while Ting Shou-chung rose to 36%. The gap between the two had narrowed to just three percentage points, and among Han's. supporters, Ko’s backing dropped by another two points. Looking at the data , this incident clearly had a significant impact. If we are talking about gaffes, the "Blue" camp didn't fare much better. On November 3rd, KMT Vice Chairman Hau Lung-bin was campaigning on Ting Shou-chung's rally stage when he accidentally shouted " Defeat Ting Shou-chung," which instantly became a nationwide......laughingstock. On November 10th, the televised debate hosted by the Public Television Service began. It was the only debate before the election where all five candidates appeared. But the biggest winner of the.

debate wasn't Ko Wen-je, Ting Shou-chung , or Yao Wen-chih, who choked up in tears—it was Wu E-yang, a former life insurance worker who paid a 2- million-dollar deposit to run for mayor . The obscure Wu E-yang was unknown to everyone before the debate. No one expected him to use all his allotted speaking time to promote a drink called honey lemon. He claimed that the tumors on his face and the sweat rashes on his hands wouldn't heal with medication, but after drinking honey lemon for a month, they all vanished. After the debate, Wu E-yang even started singing right there on. stage. " >> Life is short, just a few autumns, don't stop!" "In the east, my beauty, the Yellow River flows." "Come, have a drink, don't stop until you're done!" "Letting go of the past..." This old song, "Love the Empire More. Than the Beauty" by Li Li-fen, immediately topped music streaming and KTV charts after Wu sang it. Sales at honey lemon shops across Taiwan surged by 20%overnight. Honey lemon suddenly became an elixir, becoming the most memorable episode of this entire election. After the polling blackout began on November 14th, the election race entered a state of chaotic uncertainty. Since the gap between Ting Shou-chung and Ko Wen-je was within the margin of error before the polls closed , any minor development could have become a crucial turning point in the election. On the night of November 17th , during the Golden Horse Awards. ceremony, documentary director Fu Yue said in her acceptance speech that she hoped Taiwan would be treated as an independent entity. Shortly after, Chinese director Tu Men took the stage to present an award and said he was " honored to come to China Taipei for the Golden Horse Awards," adding that he " felt the closeness of the two sides of the strait." This immediately brought Ko Wen-je's past "one family on both sides of the strait" remarks back into the spotlight by the pan-green camp. Yao Wen-chih immediately questioned Ko: "Do you still support the 'one family' idea ?" Ko Wen-je chose not to discuss it further. Over the next few days, Yao Wen-chih launched daily inquiries, digging up Ko's past writings in a National Taiwan University Hospital publication that suggested he run for. president, pressing him on who asked him to run and which Chinese official pressured him to do so. For Yao Wen-chih , his campaign remained in a trailing position, and he was frequently turned into meme material by netizens, making his entire campaign feel sluggish and weak. For example, in an attempt to project an image of being an animal lover, Yao held a cat for a photo shoot . However, because he failed to properly support the cat's hindquarters, his posture looked just like he was holding a machine gun, instantly turning him into an internet laughingstock. He later stated publicly that because his wife was pregnant and allergic, he had given his adult cat away to a friend, which once again crossed the line for cat. lovers. Fumbling with a cat was enough to land Yao Wen-chih in a public relations crisis. The campaign became stagnant, leading many in his party to continue flirting with Ko Wen-je's camp . This is why Yao felt compelled to relentlessly attack Ko on issues like unification-independence and organ trafficking, moving toward a staunch, deep-green route to ensure the green base remained intact and to prevent himself from being the target of strategic voting. Before the election, Yao Wen-chih made a bold move, publicly pledging to resign from his position as a legislator to demonstrate his determination to fight until the end. At his campaign rally, President Tsai Ing-wen and Premier Lai Ching-te both. appeared to show their full support for Yao Wen-chih. They told everyone there was no such thing as strategic voting, but at that very moment, Ko Wen-je's wife, Chen Pei-chi, went to the Taichung World Flora Exposition and appeared alongside Lin Chia-lung's wife, making the relationship between the green and white camps seem ambiguous once again. Even at this late stage, Taipei's green voters remained hesitant and torn between Ko and Yao. Looking back. For Ko Wen-je’s camp, there was absolutely no room for optimism before the election. Internal polls showed that about a week before the vote, his lead was overtaken by Ting Shou-chung, leaving him trailing by.

three percentage points. When leading, one can campaign with relative ease, but with the race now at risk of a reversal and lacking the backing of party resources, he had no choice but to play the underdog card. Ko Wen-je calls this move the "thousand-mile raid" tactic: appearing at fruit and fish markets at the crack of dawn, visiting commercial districts to canvass office workers during the day, and hitting night markets and shopping areas in the afternoon and evening. He conducted at least seven to eight campaign stops a day, livestreaming every event to capture the turnout and making time to take photos with supporters, hoping they would post them online to create a. bandwagon effect and turn them into his "virtual" canvassers. Three days before the election, on the evening of November 21st, Ko followed the path taken by Han Kuo-yu years earlier and appeared on " Gym" Chen Chih-han's livestream. At its peak, over 70,000 people were watching simultaneously. This pre-election broadcast was like an online rally, pushing Ko's visibility to a new peak. On the eve of the election, Ko warned his supporters that if the Blue and Green camps each pulled away just a few votes, he would likely lose the election . This was no bluff, because we all know very well that a final election battle must be fought down to the very last. ball before a winner can be declared. November 24th, the moment of destiny— election day had finally arrived. On this day, the entire country was voting for mayors, councilors, and borough wardens, on top of ten referendums. As a result, long lines formed at many polling stations in Taipei early in the morning, with the average person waiting anywhere from half an hour to an hour. The Election Commission had estimated that each person would finish voting in a minute and a half, but that turned out to be a complete miscalculation! Regulations stated that anyone in line by 4:00 PM could still vote. As 4:00 PM struck, some polling stations began counting ballots while others still had crowds waiting to vote. This led to the most chaotic voting and counting scene. in history: voting and counting happened simultaneously, and those waiting in line could actually follow the live vote counts on their phones. It essentially allowed voters who hadn't cast their ballots yet to watch the results and decide whether to strategically abandon their preferred candidate. Both the Ting Shou-chung and Yao Wen-chih camps alleged that the chaotic ballot counting led voters to abandon other candidates to save Ko Wen-je, ultimately benefiting him. However, Ko's camp argued that because there were too many referendum questions, long queues formed at polling stations, causing many young people to give up on voting. Since these individuals were mostly Ko's supporters. , his camp emphasized that this chaos was actually to his disadvantage. And so , the ballot counting process was delayed by the referendums, with the vote counts between Ko Wen-je and Ting Shou-chung constantly seesawing within a range of a few hundred votes. Ko originally planned to hold a press conference at 8:00 PM, but as 9:00 PM and 10:00 PM passed without a clear winner, people grew increasingly anxious . Eventually, they decided to head out to the Ko Wen-je camp's election night party, located at the Four-Four South Village. After midnight, the results for almost every county and city across Taiwan had been finalized, leaving Taipei City as the only one where the vote count remained in a state of suspense. By 2:00 AM, the number of. people simultaneously watching the live broadcast from Ko Wen-je's headquarters surpassed 200,000. Everyone was pulling out calculators, multiplying the remaining ballot boxes by the number of voters to estimate the narrow margin and determine if a turnaround was still possible. It was just 2:20 AM on November 25th, and the ballot counting was nearly complete. At this moment, Ting Shou-chung took the stage first to announce that he would not accept the election results. He criticized the practice of counting votes while people were still casting them as an illegal election and declared that he would immediately file a lawsuit to invalidate the election. About 20 minutes later, the Central Election Commission's numbers were finally released. Ko Wen-je. secured 580,000 votes with 41%of the total, while Ting Shou-chung took 577,000 votes with 40.8%, a margin of only 3,000 votes between the two. As for the DPP's nominee, Yao Wen-chih, he received 240,000 votes, marking the worst performance for the DPP in a Taipei mayoral race since 1994. After successfully defeating both the Blue and Green parties, Ko Wen-je shouted to his supporters on-site, "The uncle is back! " Although the supporters at the scene were excited, the 11-hour marathon of ballot counting had left everyone completely exhausted. I still remember that our campaign team had long ago booked a karaoke room and an izakaya,.

intending to either celebrate or mourn our unemployment. But once the counting ended and the venue was cleared, there was suddenly only a breakfast shop left to go to, and everyone was totally wiped out. In fact, this marathon that lasted until dawn......the game wasn't over yet . Ting Shou-chung later applied for a recount, and Ko and Ting clashed once again. The recount results showed that Ting actually lost an additional 313 votes, with the margin widening to 3,567 votes. As for the subsequent lawsuits to invalidate the election, the Ting camp also demanded a recount, eventually becoming the man netizens describe as being trapped in the time rift of November 24, 2018. As for Yao Wen-chih,. he kept his word and honored his promise , truly retiring from politics after his defeat to pivot toward film, where he founded a production company. In 2022, Yao Wen-chih released his first film as a producer, "Mataro 15." Looking back at this campaign, you will find that Ko Wen-je was undoubtedly the person who utilized internet and social media elements to their absolute limit in this race. Not only did he collaborate with YouTubers to successfully broaden his reach, he was also rare among politicians for posting his own unflattering photos on Instagram, which brought him many new "Ko fans" distinct from the traditional pan-green. supporters of 2014, thereby opening a new persona for Ko. He transformed from the stern "Ko-pi" of the past into the approachable "Uncle," a term that became Ko Wen-je's brand-new nickname starting from the 2017 Universiade. The "Han Wave ," a tsunami of public opinion, swept across Taiwan, leaving the DPP with a crushing defeat and only six cities and counties under their governance. After the election, Tsai Ing-wen also traveled across the country to launch a listening tour. On December 13, she and Ko Wen-je held a historic "North Gate Meeting" at Taipei's North Gate. This meeting drew attention because of Ko Wen-je’s attitude, which the media interpreted as wearing a sour face throughout, with. almost zero interaction with Tsai Ing-wen during the discussion. However, this North Gate Meeting became a turning point for both sides; in 2019, Tsai Ing-wen came from behind in the party primary and eventually defeated Han Kuo-yu in the 2020 presidential election to win re-election, reversing the trends of 2018. As for Ko Wen-je, although he once intended to challenge for the presidency in 2019, he ultimately did not register due to considerations of political reality. Yet, in August of the same year, Ko Wen-je founded the Taiwan People's Party, allowing his political momentum to stay alive, and in their 2020 debut, they won five legislative seats, becoming the newest symbol of the. third force. In short, this election tells us that online buzz can boost your visibility, but it doesn't necessarily secure every vote for you; a stray video , or even scrolling through a breaking election report while queuing to vote, could change a person's decision the moment they step into the voting booth. On November 24, 2018, were you waiting in line outside the polling station, or were you glued to the TV watching the vote count until dawn? After midnight, the results for almost every county and city across Taiwan had been finalized, leaving Taipei City as the only one where the vote count remained in a state of suspense. By 2:00 AM, the number of. people simultaneously watching the live broadcast from Ko Wen-je's headquarters surpassed 200,000. Everyone was pulling out calculators, multiplying the remaining ballot boxes by the number of voters to estimate the narrow margin and determine if a turnaround was still possible. It was just 2:20 AM on November 25th, and the ballot counting was nearly complete. At this moment, Ting Shou-chung took the stage first to announce that he would not accept the election results. He criticized the practice of counting votes while people were still casting them as an illegal election and declared that he would immediately file a lawsuit to invalidate the election. About 20 minutes later, the Central Election Commission's numbers were finally released. Ko Wen-je. secured 580,000 votes with 41%of the total, while Ting Shou-chung took 577,000 votes with 40.8%, a margin of only 3,000 votes between the two. As for the DPP's nominee, Yao Wen-chih, he received 240,000 votes, marking the worst performance for the DPP in a Taipei mayoral race since 1994. After successfully defeating both the Blue and Green parties, Ko Wen-je shouted to his supporters on-site, "The uncle is back! " Although the supporters at the scene were excited, the 11-hour marathon of ballot counting had left everyone completely exhausted. I still remember that our campaign team had long ago booked a karaoke room and an izakaya,.

intending to either celebrate or mourn our unemployment. But once the counting ended and the venue was cleared, there was suddenly only a breakfast shop left to go to, and everyone was totally wiped out. In fact, this marathon that lasted until dawn......the game wasn't over yet . Ting Shou-chung later applied for a recount, and Ko and Ting clashed once again. The recount results showed that Ting actually lost an additional 313 votes, with the margin widening to 3,567 votes. As for the subsequent lawsuits to invalidate the election, the Ting camp also demanded a recount, eventually becoming the man netizens describe as being trapped in the time rift of November 24, 2018. As for Yao Wen-chih,. he kept his word and honored his promise , truly retiring from politics after his defeat to pivot toward film, where he founded a production company. In 2022, Yao Wen-chih released his first film as a producer, "Mataro 15." Looking back at this campaign, you will find that Ko Wen-je was undoubtedly the person who utilized internet and social media elements to their absolute limit in this race. Not only did he collaborate with YouTubers to successfully broaden his reach, he was also rare among politicians for posting his own unflattering photos on Instagram, which brought him many new "Ko fans" distinct from the traditional pan-green. supporters of 2014, thereby opening a new persona for Ko. He transformed from the stern "Ko-pi" of the past into the approachable "Uncle," a term that became Ko Wen-je's brand-new nickname starting from the 2017 Universiade. The "Han Wave ," a tsunami of public opinion, swept across Taiwan, leaving the DPP with a crushing defeat and only six cities and counties under their governance. After the election, Tsai Ing-wen also traveled across the country to launch a listening tour. On December 13, she and Ko Wen-je held a historic "North Gate Meeting" at Taipei's North Gate. This meeting drew attention because of Ko Wen-je’s attitude, which the media interpreted as wearing a sour face throughout, with. almost zero interaction with Tsai Ing-wen during the discussion. However, this North Gate Meeting became a turning point for both sides; in 2019, Tsai Ing-wen came from behind in the party primary and eventually defeated Han Kuo-yu in the 2020 presidential election to win re-election, reversing the trends of 2018. As for Ko Wen-je, although he once intended to challenge for the presidency in 2019, he ultimately did not register due to considerations of political reality. Yet, in August of the same year, Ko Wen-je founded the Taiwan People's Party, allowing his political momentum to stay alive, and in their 2020 debut, they won five legislative seats, becoming the newest symbol of the. third force. In short, this election tells us that online buzz can boost your visibility, but it doesn't necessarily secure every vote for you; a stray video , or even scrolling through a breaking election report while queuing to vote, could change a person's decision the moment they step into the voting booth.   • 解析2017年台北世界大學運動會如何從危機轉變為柯文哲聲勢回升的轉捩點。
  • 剖析2018年台北市長選舉前夕，藍綠白三方競合走向分裂與各陣營的提名決策。

摘要

柯文哲初任市長的政策考驗與民意低潮

作者回顧，柯文哲於2014年當選台北市長後，雖迅速拆除忠孝西路公車專用道贏得肯定，但隨後的「五大弊案」調查成效不如預期，且於2015年取消每年1500元的重陽敬老禮金，引發長者不滿。2016年推動「三橫三縱」自行車道工程更導致嚴重的交通瓶頸。引述旺旺中時民調指出，其滿意度一度降至40%左右，施政步調面臨嚴峻挑戰。

2017世大運的危機化解與聲勢回溫

作者指出，原本籌備期間未受高度關注的2017年台北世大運，開幕日遭遇反年改抗爭阻礙選手進場，引發社會廣泛矚目。危機化解後，柯文哲在社群網路的強硬回應獲得大量關注，配合台灣選手打破紀錄的優異表現以及「回家比賽」的宣傳訴求，激起全民熱情。世大運圓滿落幕後，柯文哲的施政滿意度回升至60%，成為其首屆任期的重要成就。

兩岸論述引發分歧與綠白政黨競合

作者提到，柯文哲在雙城論壇提及「兩岸一家親」等論述，使綠營基層對其產生質疑。在2018年市長選舉布局中，國民黨由爭取多年的丁守中贏得初選；民進黨方面，在蔡英文拋出「台灣價值」檢驗、黨內發起反柯遊行等壓力下，最終由時任總統府秘書長陳菊定調維護政黨主體性，促使民進黨決定自行提名，導致綠白合作走向終局。

I want to formally stay in my current position. >> Okay, that's enough, that's enough. You can, you can be. Yes, that's right. As you can see from this election series, today we are going to talk about the 2018 Taipei mayoral election. That’s. right, you all look like you’re sitting in front of your screens waiting for a good show, wondering what attitude I’ll take to face this episode, right? As a professional storyteller and nostalgic YouTuber, we naturally minimize our own presence and just focus on doing the job of a storyteller. So, let’s hop into a time machine today and start our story from October 29, 2014, the day Ko Wen-je defeated the long-ruling KMT to be elected mayor of Taipei. On his first day in office, Ko Wen-je demolished the abandoned and never-used Zhongxiao West Road bus lane. This swift and decisive action immediately won him applause, but. the applause didn't last very long. Shortly after taking office, Ko immediately launched an investigation into the "five major scandals," hoping to clean up before building anew. Unexpectedly, it ended up being all thunder but little rain, with very few actual problems uncovered. Although the Ko administration argued it was cleaning up issues left by Hau Lung-bin and Ma Ying-jeou, the higher the public’s expectations, the greater the disappointment. Finally, in 2015, Ko announced the cancellation of the annual 1,500 NTD Chung Yeung senior citizen subsidy. Although this move saved the city treasury 700 million NTD each year , it nearly ignited the fury of all the senior citizens in Taipei. Furthermore,. what truly impacted Ko Wen-je's approval rating was the traffic issue. In 2016, Ko pushed for the "three horizontal, three vertical" bicycle lane project. Because multiple sections were under construction simultaneously, it caused a massive traffic disaster throughout Taipei. Citizens stuck on the road complained wildly, and city councilors joined in to blast the municipal team for being inflexible. According to Want Want China Times polls, Ko's satisfaction rating fell below 50%to 40 %, and 60%of citizens felt Taipei's traffic problem was severe. For the vast number of middle-class citizens and vested interests in Taipei, these municipal actions disrupted the pace of. their accustomed lives. During its preparation, the games were not widely favored; a week before the opening, polls showed nearly 80%of Taipei citizens didn't even know the city was hosting it, but an. unexpected incident quickly made the event the focus of national attention. On August 19, 2017, the day of the opening ceremony, a group of retired military, civil, and teaching personnel protesting pension reforms broke through police barricades, threw smoke bombs, and blocked the athletes from entering the stadium. This disruption caused the athletes from various countries, who were supposed to enter to cheers, to disappear, leaving only flag-bearers to circle the field; a major international event was nearly ruined by these protesters. Fortunately, the crisis was resolved; after police cleared the. protesters, the athletes entered the stadium at the last minute, and despite the imperfect opening ceremony, it still concluded successfully. The next day, a comment appeared on Ko Wen-je’s official Facebook page, asking him directly: you guaranteed there would be no problems with the Universiade, but there was a disaster—so who is the real scumbag? Ko Wen-je replied without any hesitation: " You and those anti-pension reform groups ..." This comment scared his staff to death, but it ended up receiving over 500,000 likes! The disturbance by the protesters not only failed to embarrass Ko Wen-je or Tsai Ing-wen, but actually.

made the games the center of public attention. As Taiwanese athletes broke world records and won gold medals, all of Taiwan was ignited by the passion and excitement on the field; even track and field, usually considered a niche sport in Taiwan, drew packed crowds to the stadium thanks to the stellar performances of athletes like Cheng Chao-tsun. Under the coordination of then-Secretary-General Su Li-chiung, the slogan "We're going home to compete" fully triggered the public's intense interest in the Universiade. After the Universiade, Ko Wen-je’s approval rating soared back to 60%, and an event. originally written off became the crowning achievement of his first term. However, just as Ko Wen-je’s popularity reached its peak, the rift between him and the Green camp grew even deeper. This was because, just over a month before the Universiade, Ko Wen-je had attended the 的 双城 論壇 (Twin City Forum) in Shanghai, where he once again mentioned his "two sides of the strait are one family" rhetoric and added a proposal to build a "cross-strait community with a shared destiny." Although Ko Wen-je claimed this goodwill gesture toward China was to ensure the success of the Universiade, the pan-green grassroots simply could not accept it. To them, the mayor they once staunchly supported had become。increasingly like a stranger. Immediately after the Universiade, the political talk show "Political Shock," hosted by Professor Dennis Peng, extensively covered the controversy over the ban on Taiwanese flags at the event . Although it was later confirmed that the Military Police were in charge of venue security and the Taipei City Government had no authority to command them, rumors persist. Deep-green and pro-independence supporters could not accept Ko's remarks, and Ko's subsequent attacks on the pan-green camp sowed the seeds for the later white-green split. For the Kuomintang, attempting to block. Ko Wen-je's reelection after the Universiade, with his popularity soaring , became an increasingly daunting task. Some in the party hoped that Legislator Chiang Wan-an, who had just turned 40, would run, as he was the only one with a chance to compete with Ko, who held strong support among young people. However, Chiang refused decisively, announcing in January 2018 that he would not run for mayor. With that, the KMT’s heavy baton finally passed to the man who refused to quit for 24 years: Ting Shou-chung. Ting had wanted to run for Taipei mayor since 1994. Over the years. , he lost to Huang Ta-chou, stepped aside for Ma Ying-jeou, and later lost to Hau Lung-bin and Sean Lien; he could be called the symbol of KMT tragedy. After 24 years, and thanks to Chiang Wan-an's refusal to run, he finally won the party primary and was chosen to officially represent the KMT in the 2018 Taipei mayoral election. Although some commentators felt that the KMT had no other options, making Ting the vanguard , his local political strength, built through many consecutive terms as a legislator in Taipei, was definitely not to be underestimated. Unlike Ko Wen-je's advantage in online "air warfare," Ting. Shou-chung relied on the KMT’s traditional "ground" organization and the inherent blue-leaning voter base, which still proved effective. Having discussed the KMT, what about the DPP? Initially, the DPP did consider cooperating with Ko Wen-je again, but the problem was that the voices within the DPP grassroots demanding no more concessions were growing louder. In January 2018, during an interview, President Tsai Ing-wen was asked whether Ko Wen-je was an ally of the DPP. Tsai responded that Ko needed to reaffirm his "Taiwan values" to gain the recognition of DPP supporters. When the phrase " Taiwan values" was thrown out, some believed that Tsai Ing-wen was pushing. the pressure of a green-white coalition back onto Ko Wen-je. After all, in 2014 , to facilitate cooperation, Tsai had shouldered most of the pressure within the party. Instead of backing Ko again, she decided to let him explain his stance to green-camp supporters himself . However, the public held different views on Tsai's introduction of "Taiwan values." Many netizens questioned whether asking people to define their own "Taiwan values" amounted to ideological screening. Phrases like " your Taiwan values are insufficient" or "upholding Taiwan values" began to turn into forms of online mockery. By this time, some in the DPP could no longer sit still. In April, Legislator Yao.

Wen-chih organized a march for his Taipei mayoral bid, calling on thousands to take to the streets. Beyond demonstrating momentum, he aimed to pressure the party headquarters to nominate their own candidate. The event was ultimately defined as an anti-Ko march, where opposing Ko Wen-je and the green-white coalition became the main demands. Facing overwhelming pressure from within the party, the person who made the final decision was Presidential Office Secretary-General Chen Chu. Chen Chu firmly insisted that the DPP should not......continue to accommodate Ko Wen-je. Beyond the fact that grassroots supporters were generally dissatisfied with him, she believed that even if the DPP were to lose, it should uphold the party's own autonomy. She made a very. direct statement: "We can be different from him." After this remark, the relationship between the green camp and the white camp had almost reached its end. Although Ko Wen-je later appeared on Green Peace Radio to apologize to those offended by his "one family on both sides of the strait" remark, this gesture was criticized by the blue camp and rejected by the green camp as well. With that, the split between the white and green camps was officially solidified. The DPP formally nominated Yao Wen-chih for mayor at the end of May . The race returned to...After the DPP confirmed Yao’s nomination, TVBS released figures: Ting Shou-chung at 33. %, Ko Wen-je at 31%, and Yao Wen-chih at 13%, marking the first time Ko had fallen behind. Among DPP supporters, 49 %backed Yao Wen-chih, while only 32% supported Ko Wen-je; the green camp's vote had been starkly split in two. In Ko Wen-je's voter demographic, the younger generation aged 20 to 39 accounted for over 50%of his support, but among seniors over 60, his support dropped to just 11%. Scholars analyze that the controversy over cutting senior welfare payments, combined with his outspoken and gaffe-prone personality, are the biggest factors behind the dissatisfaction among middle-aged and elderly groups toward Ko Wen-je. Now,. without the grassroots organizational support of the DPP, it has become incredibly difficult for Ko Wen-je to reach these voters. Without a political party or an organization, how exactly is Ko Wen-je's team supposed to fight this battle? They have to find a way to secure all their own funding and buzz. First, in 2017, Ko Wen-je filmed a video with a YouTuber to promote the Universiade and became an instant hit! At that point, his aides wondered, if they replicated this approach for promoting municipal affairs, would it be possible to create the same impact? Ko Wen-je's social media team approached Walkgame and proposed a collaboration with their signature program, "The Mayor's Aide." Ultimately, "The Mayor's. Aide" was released in early July, featuring a host following Ko Wen-je for an entire day to experience the hardships of being a political aide. The natural presentation of the program, interspersed with various bits of humor , immediately ignited online traffic. In the first three days, the average daily view count exceeded 1 million, and by August 20th, it officially surpassed 10 million, becoming YouTube's top trending video of 2018. This video almost completely swept away the decline in polls that Ko's camp had experienced in the months following the split between the "White" and "Green" camps. Later, Ko Wen-je's team proposed another collaboration with Joeman for "Joe vs. Challenge," which also hit staggering view counts, and these segments. precisely highlighted the political achievements the Ko administration wanted to promote. In "The Mayor's Aide ," they visited the renovation site of the Huanan Market, and for "Joe vs. Challenge"......they ate lunch boxes in social housing with Joeman, effortlessly and naturally bringing Ko Wen-je's policy achievements to different online platforms. Shortly after "The Mayor's Aide" went online, TVBS released another Taipei mayoral poll; Ko Wen-je jumped from 31%to 40%, a growth of nine percentage points. Ting Shou-chung dropped to 30%, turning his previous narrow lead over Ko into a double-digit deficit, while Yao Wen-chih's poll numbers were at 11%. Even more notably,. young voters flocked back to support Ko Wen-je, with his support rate among those aged 20 to 39 surging to nearly 70 %. Even among those who identify with the DPP, the proportion supporting Ko Wen-je surpassed that of the DPP’s own nominee, Yao Wen-chih, as Ko regained the support of the majority of green-leaning voters. Once momentum picked up, Ko Wen-je's next step was to raise funds. With no support from any political party or foundation, Ko decided to ask his wife......Chen Pei-chi, to take out a 20 million NTD loan against their house, providing the first pot of gold for his election campaign. After receiving the money, his campaign office officially opened in.

July, with his Facebook editor becoming the very first employee. To everyone's surprise, unlike other flashy campaign offices, the staff actually worked out of a co-working space, embracing a minimalist style—or rather, a severely modest one. This image of poverty immediately stirred up sympathy from his supporters. Within just nine hours of the small-sum fundraising website going live, they had raised over 37 million NTD, breaking the records of both Blue and Green political figures. Before the end of summer, Ko Wen-je seemed to be back on track. However, it didn't last long; the "Han Wave" created by KMT. Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Han Kuo-yu began blowing north from Kaohsiung starting in late August. We have already covered the Han Wave in previous episodes, so we won't go into detail here. Han Kuo-yu’s personal charisma and his frequent soundbites directly drove ratings and web traffic, no matter what . Whether it was news praising him or commentary criticizing him, anything related to Han Kuo-yu drew huge audiences. At the time, the two major evening political talk shows, "Critical Moment" and "News Tornado," practically became fan channels for Han because their ratings were so impressive. If one could argue that web traffic might be influenced by China, then traditional TV. ratings should be enough to prove that the Han Wave was real. The person hit hardest by this Han Wave was Ko Wen-je, who was also campaigning that year; desperately needing web traffic and visibility, he was almost completely overshadowed, his media coverage cut in half, and online traffic all centered on Han Kuo-yu. This also fully awakened the previously stagnant Blue camp supporters , and even Ting Shou-chung, who had been mocked for his "Zen-like" campaign, saw his standing rise along with the tide. According to a TVBS poll in mid-September, Ko Wen-je was at 37%and Ting Shou-chung at 32%; the gap between the Blue and White camps shrank from 10 %to just 5 percentage points, proving. that this wave had spillover effects. By October, the Ko Wen-je camp dropped another bombshell, if everyone remembers . As we mentioned in the last episode, Lien Sheng-wen publicly cited the book " The Slaughter," written by an American investigative journalist, during a debate to accuse his opponent, Ko Wen-je , of involvement in organ trafficking in China. Back then, Ko Wen-je produced a lawyer's letter from the author of*The Slaughter*to successfully defeat Sean Lien. Unexpectedly, four years later, the book's author, Dr. Gutmann, arrived in Taiwan to hold an international press conference. This time, however, he pointed his finger at Ko Wen-je,. accusing him of acting as a middleman in China's organ transplant industry and even teaching Chinese doctors how to use ECMO in transplants, labeling Ko as one of the culprits behind live organ harvesting. At the scene, a member of the public asked Gutmann if he considered Ko Wen-je a liar, and he answered directly. Gutmann's personal appearance and his 180-degree shift in stance stunned everyone, especially since his lawyer's letter four years prior had endorsed Ko as a man of moral courage. Ko Wen-je's camp quickly filed a lawsuit against Gutmann and lashed out , calling him an election mercenary. This organ donation storm did not affect. Ko's momentum. According to an October survey by the Taiwan Public Opinion Foundation, only 19%of Taipei citizens agreed with Gutmann's claims, while as many as 60%disagreed. At the time, even Premier Lai Ching-te stepped forward, immediately setting the tone by stating that he believed Ko Wen-je. However, Yao Wen-chih, who was third in the polls, chose to take a gamble by biting directly into the controversy surrounding Ko's organ transplants. He argued that Ko's answers and Gutmann's accusations were at odds, with Ko dodging questions. He said if Ko could publicly condemn the CCP for harvesting organs from Falun Gong practitioners, he would publicly apologize to Ko; otherwise, he would continue to publicly. question the matter. It wasn't just Yao Wen-chih who jumped on the organ transplant controversy; even Ting Shou-chung didn't let it go, demanding that Ko publicly clarify the dispute. DPP elder Lin Cho-shui publicly rebuked Yao Wen-chih, stating that while this radical path might bring deep-green voters back, the cost would be that light-green and independent voters would all drift toward Ko Wen-je. Regarding Ting Shou-chung mentioned earlier, another municipal project he aggressively attacked was the Taipei Dome controversy. After Ko Wen-je took office, the Taipei Dome was ordered to stop construction by the city government due to deviations from the original blueprints, turning it into a massive ruin in the city center. Ting criticized Ko, saying he lacks the guts to tear it down and the nerve to finish it. He claimed that if he were mayor, he could easily resolve the Taipei Dome controversy within two months of taking office. Meanwhile, the Ko Wen-je team chose to face voters directly. On October 11, the campaign launched an online show, "Uncle Face-to-Face," borrowing the popular international car-interview format to invite citizens into a vehicle for a direct conversation with Ko, tackling issues like the Taipei Dome controversy, the cancellation of senior citizen subsidies, and whether Ko is anti-business or anti-wealth, allowing these questions to be asked openly. This approach not only drove traffic but also addressed various outside doubts regarding Ko Wen-je's governance. Speaking of the air war, the most interesting event during this period was a rap battle. On October 7, the Ting Shou-chung camp released a rap campaign song, "Taipei's Future is in Our Hands," using a pun on "Ting" and " in hand." It hit 100,000 views in one day, but was immediately criticized by. producer Hsu Chang-te, who remarked that turning rap into a rhythmic folk rhyme would only hurt their own listeners. The Ting camp remained unfazed, believing that as long as the song was catchy, it achieved its purpose. Three weeks later , Ko Wen-je released his first single, collaborating with hip-hop label Colours and rapper Chun-yen. His catchphrase, " It’s weird," became part of the song, sounding surprisingly like a real rap track. One was mocked as a rhythmic folk rhyme, while the other was dubbed by netizens as a hip-hop superstar delayed by his medical career; the gap between the two sides in the youth battlefield was clear. However, no matter how brilliantly the air war is fought, Ko. Wen-je's greatest enemy remains his own mouth. Again, on October 20, during a youth forum discussing aesthetics, he blurted out that Japanese women always wear makeup before going out, unlike some Taiwanese women who go out in public looking frightening. As soon as he said this, the audience gasped; Ko himself took it lightly, laughing that he had "spoken out of turn" again. Just as one wave subsided, another rose. A week later, on October 27, while speaking with the chairwoman of the National Women's League, Ko said, "The League is operating well now, why care about what they did in the past?" Since the Women's League has long been seen as. a KMT affiliate and part of the party's assets, this remark was viewed by the Pan-Green camp as a denial of transitional justice, turning many of his supporters into critics. Ko’s troubles didn't end there. On November 5 , his campaign director, writer Hsiao Yeh, appeared in a campaign video for Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Chen Chi-mai , publicly endorsing him. As soon as this video was released, it infuriated many light-blue voters who supported both Han Kuo-yu and Ko. They believed Han Kuo-yu treated Ko Wen-je with loyalty, choosing not to come to Taipei to support Ting Shou-chung. Despite. repeated invitations from the Ting camp hoping to bring the "Han Wave" to Taipei , Han declined them all out of gratitude for Ko’s past help. Yet, Ko Wen-je unexpectedly let his own campaign manager film a video endorsing Chen Chi-mai. The outraged comments from Han's supporters nearly flooded Ko’s social media posts. His camp later claimed it was a personal endorsement of Chen Chi-mai and had nothing to do with Ko, but the damage to his polling numbers had already been done. According to mid-November TVBS polling data, Ko Wen-je’s support stood at 39%, while Ting Shou-chung rose to 36%. The gap between the two had narrowed to just three percentage points, and among Han's. supporters, Ko’s backing dropped by another two points. Looking at the data , this incident clearly had a significant impact. If we are talking about gaffes, the "Blue" camp didn't fare much better. On November 3rd, KMT Vice Chairman Hau Lung-bin was campaigning on Ting Shou-chung's rally stage when he accidentally shouted " Defeat Ting Shou-chung," which instantly became a nationwide......laughingstock. On November 10th, the televised debate hosted by the Public Television Service began. It was the only debate before the election where all five candidates appeared. But the biggest winner of the.

debate wasn't Ko Wen-je, Ting Shou-chung , or Yao Wen-chih, who choked up in tears—it was Wu E-yang, a former life insurance worker who paid a 2- million-dollar deposit to run for mayor . The obscure Wu E-yang was unknown to everyone before the debate. No one expected him to use all his allotted speaking time to promote a drink called honey lemon. He claimed that the tumors on his face and the sweat rashes on his hands wouldn't heal with medication, but after drinking honey lemon for a month, they all vanished. After the debate, Wu E-yang even started singing right there on. stage. " >> Life is short, just a few autumns, don't stop!" "In the east, my beauty, the Yellow River flows." "Come, have a drink, don't stop until you're done!" "Letting go of the past..." This old song, "Love the Empire More. Than the Beauty" by Li Li-fen, immediately topped music streaming and KTV charts after Wu sang it. Sales at honey lemon shops across Taiwan surged by 20%overnight. Honey lemon suddenly became an elixir, becoming the most memorable episode of this entire election. After the polling blackout began on November 14th, the election race entered a state of chaotic uncertainty. Since the gap between Ting Shou-chung and Ko Wen-je was within the margin of error before the polls closed , any minor development could have become a crucial turning point in the election. On the night of November 17th , during the Golden Horse Awards. ceremony, documentary director Fu Yue said in her acceptance speech that she hoped Taiwan would be treated as an independent entity. Shortly after, Chinese director Tu Men took the stage to present an award and said he was " honored to come to China Taipei for the Golden Horse Awards," adding that he " felt the closeness of the two sides of the strait." This immediately brought Ko Wen-je's past "one family on both sides of the strait" remarks back into the spotlight by the pan-green camp. Yao Wen-chih immediately questioned Ko: "Do you still support the 'one family' idea ?" Ko Wen-je chose not to discuss it further. Over the next few days, Yao Wen-chih launched daily inquiries, digging up Ko's past writings in a National Taiwan University Hospital publication that suggested he run for. president, pressing him on who asked him to run and which Chinese official pressured him to do so. For Yao Wen-chih , his campaign remained in a trailing position, and he was frequently turned into meme material by netizens, making his entire campaign feel sluggish and weak. For example, in an attempt to project an image of being an animal lover, Yao held a cat for a photo shoot . However, because he failed to properly support the cat's hindquarters, his posture looked just like he was holding a machine gun, instantly turning him into an internet laughingstock. He later stated publicly that because his wife was pregnant and allergic, he had given his adult cat away to a friend, which once again crossed the line for cat. lovers. Fumbling with a cat was enough to land Yao Wen-chih in a public relations crisis. The campaign became stagnant, leading many in his party to continue flirting with Ko Wen-je's camp . This is why Yao felt compelled to relentlessly attack Ko on issues like unification-independence and organ trafficking, moving toward a staunch, deep-green route to ensure the green base remained intact and to prevent himself from being the target of strategic voting. Before the election, Yao Wen-chih made a bold move, publicly pledging to resign from his position as a legislator to demonstrate his determination to fight until the end. At his campaign rally, President Tsai Ing-wen and Premier Lai Ching-te both. appeared to show their full support for Yao Wen-chih. They told everyone there was no such thing as strategic voting, but at that very moment, Ko Wen-je's wife, Chen Pei-chi, went to the Taichung World Flora Exposition and appeared alongside Lin Chia-lung's wife, making the relationship between the green and white camps seem ambiguous once again. Even at this late stage, Taipei's green voters remained hesitant and torn between Ko and Yao. Looking back. For Ko Wen-je’s camp, there was absolutely no room for optimism before the election. Internal polls showed that about a week before the vote, his lead was overtaken by Ting Shou-chung, leaving him trailing by.

three percentage points. When leading, one can campaign with relative ease, but with the race now at risk of a reversal and lacking the backing of party resources, he had no choice but to play the underdog card. Ko Wen-je calls this move the "thousand-mile raid" tactic: appearing at fruit and fish markets at the crack of dawn, visiting commercial districts to canvass office workers during the day, and hitting night markets and shopping areas in the afternoon and evening. He conducted at least seven to eight campaign stops a day, livestreaming every event to capture the turnout and making time to take photos with supporters, hoping they would post them online to create a. bandwagon effect and turn them into his "virtual" canvassers. Three days before the election, on the evening of November 21st, Ko followed the path taken by Han Kuo-yu years earlier and appeared on " Gym" Chen Chih-han's livestream. At its peak, over 70,000 people were watching simultaneously. This pre-election broadcast was like an online rally, pushing Ko's visibility to a new peak. On the eve of the election, Ko warned his supporters that if the Blue and Green camps each pulled away just a few votes, he would likely lose the election . This was no bluff, because we all know very well that a final election battle must be fought down to the very last. ball before a winner can be declared. November 24th, the moment of destiny— election day had finally arrived. On this day, the entire country was voting for mayors, councilors, and borough wardens, on top of ten referendums. As a result, long lines formed at many polling stations in Taipei early in the morning, with the average person waiting anywhere from half an hour to an hour. The Election Commission had estimated that each person would finish voting in a minute and a half, but that turned out to be a complete miscalculation! Regulations stated that anyone in line by 4:00 PM could still vote. As 4:00 PM struck, some polling stations began counting ballots while others still had crowds waiting to vote. This led to the most chaotic voting and counting scene. in history: voting and counting happened simultaneously, and those waiting in line could actually follow the live vote counts on their phones. It essentially allowed voters who hadn't cast their ballots yet to watch the results and decide whether to strategically abandon their preferred candidate. Both the Ting Shou-chung and Yao Wen-chih camps alleged that the chaotic ballot counting led voters to abandon other candidates to save Ko Wen-je, ultimately benefiting him. However, Ko's camp argued that because there were too many referendum questions, long queues formed at polling stations, causing many young people to give up on voting. Since these individuals were mostly Ko's supporters. , his camp emphasized that this chaos was actually to his disadvantage. And so , the ballot counting process was delayed by the referendums, with the vote counts between Ko Wen-je and Ting Shou-chung constantly seesawing within a range of a few hundred votes. Ko originally planned to hold a press conference at 8:00 PM, but as 9:00 PM and 10:00 PM passed without a clear winner, people grew increasingly anxious . Eventually, they decided to head out to the Ko Wen-je camp's election night party, located at the Four-Four South Village. After midnight, the results for almost every county and city across Taiwan had been finalized, leaving Taipei City as the only one where the vote count remained in a state of suspense. By 2:00 AM, the number of. people simultaneously watching the live broadcast from Ko Wen-je's headquarters surpassed 200,000. Everyone was pulling out calculators, multiplying the remaining ballot boxes by the number of voters to estimate the narrow margin and determine if a turnaround was still possible. It was just 2:20 AM on November 25th, and the ballot counting was nearly complete. At this moment, Ting Shou-chung took the stage first to announce that he would not accept the election results. He criticized the practice of counting votes while people were still casting them as an illegal election and declared that he would immediately file a lawsuit to invalidate the election. About 20 minutes later, the Central Election Commission's numbers were finally released. Ko Wen-je. secured 580,000 votes with 41%of the total, while Ting Shou-chung took 577,000 votes with 40.8%, a margin of only 3,000 votes between the two. As for the DPP's nominee, Yao Wen-chih, he received 240,000 votes, marking the worst performance for the DPP in a Taipei mayoral race since 1994. After successfully defeating both the Blue and Green parties, Ko Wen-je shouted to his supporters on-site, "The uncle is back! " Although the supporters at the scene were excited, the 11-hour marathon of ballot counting had left everyone completely exhausted. I still remember that our campaign team had long ago booked a karaoke room and an izakaya,.

intending to either celebrate or mourn our unemployment. But once the counting ended and the venue was cleared, there was suddenly only a breakfast shop left to go to, and everyone was totally wiped out. In fact, this marathon that lasted until dawn......the game wasn't over yet . Ting Shou-chung later applied for a recount, and Ko and Ting clashed once again. The recount results showed that Ting actually lost an additional 313 votes, with the margin widening to 3,567 votes. As for the subsequent lawsuits to invalidate the election, the Ting camp also demanded a recount, eventually becoming the man netizens describe as being trapped in the time rift of November 24, 2018. As for Yao Wen-chih,. he kept his word and honored his promise , truly retiring from politics after his defeat to pivot toward film, where he founded a production company. In 2022, Yao Wen-chih released his first film as a producer, "Mataro 15." Looking back at this campaign, you will find that Ko Wen-je was undoubtedly the person who utilized internet and social media elements to their absolute limit in this race. Not only did he collaborate with YouTubers to successfully broaden his reach, he was also rare among politicians for posting his own unflattering photos on Instagram, which brought him many new "Ko fans" distinct from the traditional pan-green. supporters of 2014, thereby opening a new persona for Ko. He transformed from the stern "Ko-pi" of the past into the approachable "Uncle," a term that became Ko Wen-je's brand-new nickname starting from the 2017 Universiade. The "Han Wave ," a tsunami of public opinion, swept across Taiwan, leaving the DPP with a crushing defeat and only six cities and counties under their governance. After the election, Tsai Ing-wen also traveled across the country to launch a listening tour. On December 13, she and Ko Wen-je held a historic "North Gate Meeting" at Taipei's North Gate. This meeting drew attention because of Ko Wen-je’s attitude, which the media interpreted as wearing a sour face throughout, with. almost zero interaction with Tsai Ing-wen during the discussion. However, this North Gate Meeting became a turning point for both sides; in 2019, Tsai Ing-wen came from behind in the party primary and eventually defeated Han Kuo-yu in the 2020 presidential election to win re-election, reversing the trends of 2018. As for Ko Wen-je, although he once intended to challenge for the presidency in 2019, he ultimately did not register due to considerations of political reality. Yet, in August of the same year, Ko Wen-je founded the Taiwan People's Party, allowing his political momentum to stay alive, and in their 2020 debut, they won five legislative seats, becoming the newest symbol of the. third force.
